No rib fracture or other skeletal abnormality identified in the visualized field. The cardiomediastinal silhouette appears prominent but cannot be reliably assessed on this projection.
impression: Intubated, monitored patient with diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic) and/or bilateral pneumonia, with probable small bilateral pleural effusions and basal atelectasis; endotracheal tube with a somewhat high tip position; no pneumothorax or acute skeletal injury.
limitations: Single frontal (AP, likely portable) view; no lateral view and no prior images for comparison. Costophrenic angles and the lower diaphragms are at or below the bottom edge of the field of view, so the size of any pleural effusion cannot be quantified. Multiple overlying monitoring devices (ECG leads, electrodes, external tubing) obscure parts of the lung fields. Cardiac size cannot be reliably assessed because of AP geometry and adjacent parenchymal opacity. The carina is not directly visualized; the ETT tip depth is estimated from bony/pixel landmarks. Pretrained model outputs are probabilistic and partially discordant (e.g., ResNet-512 vs DenseNet-224/jfhealthcare on cardiomegaly and effusion) and were used only as corroborating evidence; the lung segmentation mask is imperfect exactly where the lung is abnormal. Image is an 8-bit PNG without original DICOM metadata.

findings: Portable frontal (AP) chest radiograph with 'R' marker. A central venous catheter enters from the right neck (right internal jugular approach) and descends along the right paratracheal line; its clearly visible course ends in the mid-lower mediastinum at approximately the lower SVC / cavoatrial junction level, with no visible coiling, pleural course, or arterial misposition; the exact tip is not fully confirmable because of overlap with the mediastinal shadow. Prominent cardiac silhouette with a borderline cardiothoracic ratio (estimated 0.42 to 0.53, AP magnification present). Hazy, ill-defined opacity in the left lower zone / retrocardiac region, obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and the medial left costophrenic angle, most consistent with atelectasis; early consolidation or a small effusion cannot be excluded. Mild haziness at the right lung base. No definite pneumothorax (lung markings reach the pleural periphery at both apices; no pleural line). No definite pleural effusion: the right costophrenic angle is nearly sharp and the left angle is obscured by the breast shadow. Right hemidiaphragm is approximately 2 cm higher than the left, within the normal range. Trachea midline; mediastinal contours unremarkable for an AP film; no definite rib fracture or bony lesion. External monitoring devices: three ECG electrodes (two infraclavicular, one over the mid-mediastinum) with lead wires crossing both hemithoraces, and an external cable over the left lower flank.
impression: Portable AP chest radiograph with a right internal jugular central venous catheter in apparent appropriate position (visible tip at approximately lower SVC level, no malposition identified), prominent cardiac silhouette with borderline cardiomegaly, and a hazy left lower zone / retrocardiac opacity most consistent with atelectasis (early consolidation or small effusion not excluded). No pneumothorax and no definite effusion. External ECG monitoring devices overlie the thorax.
limitations: Single portable AP view without a lateral view: AP geometry magnifies the heart and widens the mediastinum, so the borderline cardiothoracic ratio cannot distinguish true cardiomegaly from projectional magnification. Breast shadows obscure the left costophrenic angle and part of the left lower lung field. Overlying ECG electrodes and wires can mimic or obscure lines and small lesions, and the mid-mediastinal electrode lies near the fading catheter. The exact catheter tip position is not confirmable because of overlap with the mediastinal shadow. The study is a PNG copy of the original radiograph with fixed windowing (values 0-240), limiting subtle contrast. Atelectasis, a small effusion, and early consolidation cannot be reliably separated on a single frontal film. Pretrained model outputs were used only as corroboration; several were partially off-distribution for this portable AP image with monitoring devices, and the 159-class anatomy segmentation model produced an incoherent map and was discarded as a documented negative result.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (PA projection). The right hemidiaphragm lies higher than the left by approximately 2 cm, at the upper limit of the normal right-over-left difference (possible mild right hemidiaphragm elevation or a normal variant). A thin, linear, tapering opacity in the left mid-lung zone runs from the left heart border toward the lateral chest wall, consistent with a fissure or minimal plate-like atelectasis. The cardiac silhouette is normal to borderline in size. The lungs are otherwise well aerated; there is no definite consolidation, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or pulmonary edema. Small punctate opacities are seen in the right lower zone / right upper quadrant (indeterminate, possibly calcifications). No lines, tubes, or devices are present.
impression: Near-normal frontal chest radiograph with no definite acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. The notable features are a relatively higher right hemidiaphragm (borderline; possibly a normal variant or mild elevation) and a thin left mid-zone linear opacity (likely a fissure or minimal atelectasis).
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view). 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata, so the exact field of view is unknown and centimetre measurements are approximate. Overlying breast shadows obscure the lower lung zones and the right costophrenic angle. The heart occludes the medial diaphragm on a frontal view, and the provided segmentation models could not reliably segment the hemidiaphragms, so the dome heights were measured by direct visual reading of a gridded image. Pretrained pathology classifiers (DenseNet/ResNet) returned scores at or just below the calibrated operating threshold with model-to-model disagreement on borderline labels; the BiomedCLIP zero-shot result is not calibrated and was used only as directional support. The small right-base punctate opacity is indeterminate without further views or imaging.

findings: Frontal (AP) chest radiograph of a patient who appears pediatric/small; the film is rotated and carries heavy external artifacts (multiple ECG cables and snap electrodes over the chest, and an external crutch/pole over the abducted left arm). The cardiac silhouette is enlarged and globular; the measured cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.64 (uncertainty band 0.59-0.69), which exceeds the normal threshold even allowing for AP projection. There is a mild-to-moderate hazy/reticular increased opacity in the bilateral mid and lower lung zones, slightly more prominent on the right, while the lung apices and upper zones are clearly aerated; there is no dense lobar consolidation or air bronchogram. The diaphragms are elevated (low lung volumes). No pneumothorax and no large pleural effusion are identified. No internal lines or tubes are present (all visible wires are external ECG/telemetry cables terminating at visible electrodes). No obvious acute bony abnormality is seen.
impression: Cardiomegaly with bilateral hazy mid-lower zone pulmonary opacities, most consistent with congestive/pulmonary-edema changes in the setting of an enlarged heart, with pneumonia a secondary consideration. Interpretation is limited by AP projection, low lung volumes, rotation and heavy external monitoring artifacts.
limitations: Single frontal AP view; no lateral view. AP projection and elevated diaphragms (low lung volumes) magnify the heart and can exaggerate parenchymal opacity. The image is rotated and overlaid by external monitoring hardware (ECG cables/electrodes, external crutch), which partially obscures the lung fields and costophrenic angles (a small effusion cannot be excluded). The film is low contrast, so the parenchymal opacity is subtle. Patient age is not stated and must be inferred from morphology (appears pediatric/small), which changes CT-ratio reference values. Several available pretrained models (xrv DenseNet/ResNet/PSPNet and the xrv view classifier, plus the wrist-fracture YOLOv8 and bone-fracture classifier) behaved out-of-distribution on this image and were excluded; the interpretation rests on direct visual inspection and the MedSAM-verified CT-ratio measurement.

findings: Portable AP (supine/semi-erect) chest radiograph of a monitored patient with low lung volumes. Bilateral hazy parenchymal opacities with basilar predominance: a dense retrocardiac opacity obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and left costophrenic angle (left lower lobe collapse and/or consolidation and/or effusion), and a hazy, obscured right base with loss of the right costophrenic angle. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, likely exaggerated by AP/supine projection. Trachea midline; no mediastinal shift. No pneumothorax; no fracture identified. Devices: multiple ECG monitoring electrodes, external IV lines, a thin line running from the left neck into the mediastinum (possible catheter), and a looped (hairpin-coiled) tubular structure with a small round radiodense focus over the left clavicle/first rib - a coiled catheter or external tubing, not definitively characterizable on a single frontal view. Dental restoration in the mandible (incidental).
impression: Bilateral pleural effusions with basilar atelectasis/consolidation, including a dense retrocardiac (left lower lobe) opacity, in a monitored patient; apparent cardiomegaly likely projectional. Findings are most consistent with fluid-overload/immobility-related changes in a critically ill patient. No pneumothorax or fracture. The looped left-infraclavicular device (catheter vs external tubing) requires clinical correlation.
limitations: Single portable AP supine view; no lateral view and no prior for comparison. Supine/AP technique magnifies the cardiac silhouette, allows free pleural fluid to layer posteriorly (extent not measurable), and causes basilar vascular crowding that can mimic edema. Multiple external devices (ECG electrodes, IV lines, looped left-infraclavicular tubing) overlie the lung fields; the looped device cannot be definitively characterized (indwelling catheter vs external tubing) without clinical correlation. AI model limitations: the supervised models disagreed in degree (DenseNet more positive than ResNet50); the segmentation models under-segmented the heart and over-segmented the diaphragm/scapulae, so a quantitative cardiothoracic ratio is unreliable; zero-shot vision-language scores are uncalibrated. Interpretation relies on the original image, with model outputs used only as supporting evidence.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely AP/portable) with four ECG electrodes and external monitoring cables overlying the chest; no indwelling central line, NG tube or chest tube is identified. Diffuse bilateral patchy airspace opacities are present in all lung zones, confluent in the left lower zone with partial silhouetting of the left hemidiaphragm and left heart border. Zone quantification (PSPNet lung masks) confirms increased density in every zone of both lungs (apical mean intensities ~89-92), with the left mid and lower zones clearly denser than the right (left lower mean 101 vs right lower 81; fraction of hyperdense pixels 41% vs 30%). A vague, ill-defined density in the right mid zone is part of the diffuse patchy process and does not correspond to a discrete nodule (ROI max intensity 115). No pneumothorax is seen. The left costophrenic angle is obscured and a small left pleural effusion cannot be excluded. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is prominent, most likely magnification from the AP projection; classifier scores argue against true cardiomegaly. No rib fractures or other acute bony abnormality.
impression: Multifocal bilateral airspace disease with left basal predominance, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia; asymmetric pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic) cannot be excluded on a single frontal view.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral or prior comparison; no DICOM metadata, so projection, patient factors and timing are unknown and AP/portable acquisition is inferred from the monitoring equipment, which also magnifies the cardiac silhouette. 8-bit PNG with moderate noise and a black band at the inferior edge. ECG electrodes and cables overlying the chest can mimic or obscure focal findings. Model outputs are supporting only: two in-domain chest X-ray classifiers were validated on this image with inverted-image negative controls (one content-insensitive classifier was rejected and not used for any finding), one vision-language model was used as a ranking only, and pneumonia versus edema cannot be separated definitively without clinical context.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph of a critically ill patient with multiple support devices (ECG leads, central venous catheter, an enteric tube coursing down the midline, and a radiopaque marker/label on the left). There is diffuse bilateral hazy alveolar and interstitial opacity with basilar predominance. The opacification is asymmetric, with greater density in the left mid and lower zones than the right (the right mid-zone is comparatively more aerated). Both costophrenic angles are obscured by basilar opacity, consistent with pleural effusion and/or basilar atelectasis/consolidation. No definite pneumothorax and no discrete, well-circumscribed mass are identified. The cardiac silhouette is not reliably assessable.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacification, most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic/ARDS) in a critically ill, supported patient, with superimposed bilateral pleural effusions and a left-predominant focal consolidation/atelectasis component.
limitations: Single 8-bit PNG of a portable AP film (not the original DICOM), with patient rotation and multiple superimposed support devices that obscure and can mimic pathology. The AP projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette, so cardiomegaly could not be reliably assessed. Pretrained models (DenseNet, ResNet, PSPNet, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM) were trained predominantly on cleaner PA films and gave divergent, partly out-of-distribution outputs; their outputs were used only as supporting evidence, and any single model score was not allowed to drive a finding. No lateral view or comparison films were available. The exact positions of the tube/line tips and the identity of the 'GJ' marker/radiopaque object are not fully characterized.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. A large, dense, homogeneous opacity in the left mid-to-lower zone obscuring the left hemidiaphragm, the left costophrenic angle, and part of the left heart border, with a superior border in the mid-zone and no definite air bronchograms; the left upper zone remains aerated. Increased interstitial/patchy opacity in the right mid-to-lower lung. A radiopaque airway tube in the cervical trachea (endotracheal or tracheostomy tube) with an adjacent midline line. Multiple external ECG electrodes. A coiled tubular device in the right lower zone and a midline tubular line (feeding tube or central venous catheter). The trachea is midline without definite mediastinal shift. No definite pneumothorax; no definite rib fracture identified.
impression: Large left basilar opacity, most consistent with a large left pleural effusion +/- left lower lobe atelectasis/consolidation, with lesser right basilar opacity (possible edema or infiltrate), in a patient with multiple support devices.
limitations: Single portable AP view (magnification and suboptimal penetration), patient rotation, and superimposed external devices limit assessment. A single frontal view cannot reliably distinguish effusion from consolidation from atelectasis, exclude mediastinal shift, or fully assess the cardiac silhouette. Pretrained model outputs (xrv DenseNet/ResNet, BiomedCLIP) are approximate, partly uncertain on this degraded image, and do not substitute for clinical correlation. A lateral view and/or thoracic ultrasound would better characterize the left opacity and the airway/line devices.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of an adult with bilateral breast shadows. (1) Right-sided implantable infusion port in the right mid chest wall (projected over the right mid lung zone, about the 4th-6th rib level): flat low-density body with two lateral suture-tab wings, each with a round hole, and a radiopaque catheter that ascends over the right lung, forms a mild loop (excess length) at the right apex, and descends along the right mediastinum; the distal tip is projected over the lower SVC/cavoatrial region but its exact position is not determinable against the cardiac silhouette. (2) A cluster of about 7 small (2-4 mm) ovoid/teardrop dense objects with dense rims and relatively lucent centers in the right mid-lower lung zone just above the right hemidiaphragm; in this 8-bit image their peak density is below bone level, so the differential includes small surgical clips (prior procedure), calcified lymph nodes/granulomas, vessels or airways on end, or small foreign bodies. (3) A hazy rounded soft-tissue opacity of about 2-2.5 cm in the left mid lung zone, abutting the left heart border, with aerated lung lateral to it; differential includes a pulmonary nodule or mass, confluent pulmonary vessels, or a pericardial/epicardial border structure. (4) A few small (2-8 mm) dense ring-like and dot-like objects near the left heart border/hilum and in the right mid lung zone. (5) No pneumothorax (apices and lateral pleura clear on lung window), no pleural effusion (both costophrenic angles sharp), no focal consolidation. (6) Cardiomediastinal silhouette normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.29 by image analysis). (7) Osseous structures intact, no acute fracture; the straight linear bands over the left heart border are rib crossings. (8) Gastric bubble present; no pneumoperitoneum seen.
impression: Single frontal chest radiograph without acute cardiopulmonary process. The main abnormality is a rounded 2-2.5 cm soft-tissue opacity in the left mid lung zone (pulmonary nodule/mass until characterized by lateral view or CT). Additionally: right-sided port-a-cath with catheter loop at the right apex and tip in the lower SVC region, and a cluster of about 7 small dense ovoid objects in the right mid-lower lung zone (most likely small surgical clips or calcified nodes).
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral) and no prior images for comparison. 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata: compressed dynamic range (bone peaks around 211/250), so thin metallic objects cannot be reliably distinguished from dense calcification and no absolute HU quantification is possible. The catheter tip is not clearly visible against the cardiac silhouette. Breast shadows overlie the lower lung zones, reducing sensitivity for basilar disease. The cardiothoracic ratio was estimated by image analysis (0.29), with the heart mask of the segmentation model under-segmented and discarded. The exact nature of the clustered ovoid objects and of the left mid-zone opacity cannot be determined on a single frontal film. Pretrained model outputs (in-domain chest classifiers and zero-shot vision-language model) were used only as supporting evidence after sanity checks; out-of-domain models (pediatric wrist detector, community bone-fracture classifier) were run and rejected as untrustworthy. CT of the chest is recommended to characterize the left mid-zone opacity and the right mid-lower cluster.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Large, well-circumscribed, rounded to lobulated soft-tissue mass in the left upper zone, projecting over the aortic arch and left hilum, with smooth convex margins; the main component measures 202x148 px (area ~22800 px^2 at 1024 px image size) and is soft-tissue dense (mean intensity 118 vs 91 in the contralateral aerated control). Structure segmentation places most of the mass within the left lung territory, with its inferior part fusing with the left heart border; the left heart border is therefore partly obscured and cardiac silhouette assessment is limited. The right lung is well aerated and clear; no definite consolidation, pleural effusion or pneumothorax. The trachea is essentially midline (no significant deviation). An irregular, mottled dense structure is projected over the right paratracheal neck (possible foreign body, calcification or external artifact; indeterminate). A faint indeterminate punctate density is present near the left mid-axillary line (likely a vessel in cross-section or minor artifact; no clinical weight). No objective evidence of an elevated fissure or lobar collapse on this view. An 'R' orientation marker and alphanumeric overlay are present in the upper left corner.
impression: Large well-circumscribed left upper zone / juxtahilar mass (intrapulmonary or paratracheal-hilar), most likely a neoplastic lesion (lymphoma if the patient is young, primary lung neoplasm if adult) or a congenital/cystic lesion (bronchogenic cyst, congenital pulmonary airway malformation); no acute parenchymal process otherwise identified. Patient habitus appears young but age could not be reliably determined from this image.
limitations: Single frontal view only; without a lateral view the mass cannot be definitively localised as intrapulmonary versus mediastinal. Patient age/sex cannot be reliably determined (visual impression suggests a young patient; zero-shot CLIP habitus prompts weakly suggest adult; no demographic model was used). Cardiac size is unassessable where the mass overlaps the left heart border. Lower lung zones are partly obscured by overlying soft tissue. No scale marker, so all sizes are in pixels. Classifier scores (DenseNet-121/224, ResNet-50/512) are calibrated operating points trained on adult cohorts and were used only as supporting evidence; PSPNet segmentation is coarse and under-calls hilar/aortic labels; MedSAM output is a prompt-dependent geometric measurement. Out-of-domain models (wrist YOLO, bone-fracture classifier) were run as negative controls and excluded as untrustworthy.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Diffuse bilateral reticulonodular/interstitial-alveolar opacities involving all lung zones, most pronounced in the mid and lower zones. Dense confluent opacity at the left base partially obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and the left heart border. Cardiac silhouette indeterminate due to overlying opacities, with borderline enlargement by model scores. No pneumothorax. No large pleural effusion; a small left basilar effusion cannot be excluded. No definite rib fracture or other acute skeletal abnormality. External artifacts: a perforated metallic arch-bar/splint-type device projecting over the mandible and oral cavity, a small ring-shaped metallic object over the right shoulder, and two ECG electrodes over the lateral chest walls. A cluster of approximately 7-8 small ring-shaped metallic densities projects over the right mid-lower lung field (surgical clips or external metallic object; identity not determinable).
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacification consistent with a diffuse parenchymal process (differential: diffuse pneumonia, pulmonary edema, or diffuse metastatic disease including lymphangitic carcinomatosis) with a dominant left lower lobe consolidation component; multiple external metallic and ECG artifacts; no acute skeletal injury identified.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral or prior comparison; hazy image with reduced contrast; cardiac size assessment limited by overlying opacities and projection; multiple external metallic/ECG artifacts; identity of the metallic cluster over the right mid-lower lung field undetermined; pretrained model scores are calibrated operating-point values, not probabilities; the segmentation model's heart mask failed and was excluded from conclusions; out-of-domain models (pediatric-wrist detector, bone-fracture classifier) misfired on this image and were excluded; zero-shot vision-language results are prompt-sensitive.

findings: Frontal (AP, likely portable/supine) chest radiograph, upper-to-mid thorax. Bilateral diffuse hazy pulmonary opacities with a reticular-interstitial and patchy-alveolar component, perihilar and lower-zone predominant, more confluent in the left mid-lower zone; the right lung shows patchy opacities with small lucent foci. Hila are indistinct. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent but cannot be reliably sized (image is cropped and AP magnification is present). Trachea is midline. No pneumothorax, no definite rib or clavicular fracture, and no definite large pleural effusion are identified (the costophrenic angles are not fully included). Multiple external ECG electrodes and monitoring lead wires overlie the chest; a thin linear structure overlying the right lung is most consistent with an external monitoring lead. An 'L' side marker is present.
impression: Abnormal: bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities. The pattern (bilateral, perihilar and lower-zone/dependent predominant, with indistinct hila) is most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic), but multifocal pneumonia or a mixed alveolar process is a close alternative; the specific etiology cannot be determined from this single cropped frontal image.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) projection cropped to the upper-mid thorax: the diaphragm and costophrenic angles are not fully included, so pleural effusion and basilar disease cannot be fully assessed and the cardiac silhouette cannot be sized (AP magnification). External ECG electrodes and monitoring leads overlie the lung fields and can mimic or obscure pathology. The image is an 8-bit (windowed) PNG rather than raw DICOM. Pretrained-model outputs are limited: classifier scores are biased by the cropped field (lower-zone and cardiac-silhouette labels are unreliable) and the models disagree on the specific etiology (edema vs pneumonia); the community bone-fracture model was not relied on (no fracture seen on inspection). Clinical and laboratory correlation is required.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of an inpatient with multiple ECG electrodes and a left-sided central venous catheter whose tip lies within the mediastinum (likely SVC/RA junction); no endotracheal tube. Diffuse bilateral airspace and interstitial opacities, more extensive on the right, with patchy right mid-lung consolidation and air bronchograms. Dense right base opacity obscures the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border (right lower zone consolidation with probable right pleural effusion). Milder reticular/ground-glass opacities in the left lung with haziness at the left base (possible small left effusion). Zone density quantification confirms right > left predominance (right base mean 152 vs left upper 78). No pneumothorax identified at the apices or chest wall. Trachea midline. No convincing cardiomegaly on this AP projection (heart/thorax width ratio ~0.51; classifier cardiomegaly scores near 0). No definite rib fracture.
impression: Diffuse bilateral airspace disease, right greater than left, with dense right base consolidation/effusion in a critically ill patient. Most consistent with multifocal pneumonia (with parapneumonic effusion) or non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema/ARDS; cardiogenic edema is less likely given the absence of cardiomegaly and low edema scores, but not excluded.
limitations: Single portable supine AP film: cardiac size is magnified, pleural fluid layers posteriorly (underestimating effusion size), and sensitivity for a small pneumothorax is reduced. Overlying ECG electrodes and the catheter obscure parts of the lung fields and the catheter tip is not fully verifiable. No prior studies for comparison. Pretrained model outputs on this inpatient image are only partially reliable (many pathology scores near the neutral operating point), so they were used solely as supporting evidence alongside direct visual inspection. Clinical and laboratory correlation is required to distinguish pneumonia from edema/ARDS.

findings: Frontal (PA, erect) chest radiograph. A large, well-circumscribed round-to-oval structure occupies the left lower hemithorax; its superior border is smooth, convex and sharply marginated, projecting up to approximately the 4th-5th anterior rib level, i.e. about 3 rib levels above the right hemidiaphragm dome (which is normally the higher side by 1-3 rib levels). The interior of the structure is of approximately aerated-lung density (slightly more lucent than adjacent lung on pixel measurement) with visible vascular/reticular markings and overlying ribs; no definite air bronchograms, fat or large air collection within it. A thin hyperlucent (gas-density) crescent runs along its inferior/inferolateral margin, and below that a dense curved band is seen at the left hemidiaphragm level, with the gastric gas bubble beneath it; the left hemidiaphragm is not identifiable as a separate thin line. A dense curved band runs along the lateral aspect of the structure. Right lung clear; left lateral costophrenic angle sharp and aerated (no pleural effusion); no pneumothorax; normal cardiomediastinal silhouette; midline trachea; no rib fracture or foreign body identified. 'L' and 'A' orientation markers are present at the top right corner.
impression: Marked elevation of the left hemidiaphragm as a large, well-defined dome-shaped structure in the left lower hemithorax with aerated contents and gas below; most likely left diaphragmatic eventration or phrenic nerve palsy, or a left diaphragmatic (Bochdalek) hernia containing aerated bowel - not separable on a single frontal view. No other acute intrathoracic abnormality identified.
limitations: Single frontal projection only; no lateral view, so the relationship of the dome to the posterior costophrenic sulcus and the thoracic versus subdiaphragmatic location of its contents cannot be established; CT (or a lateral/contrast study) would be required for a definitive diagnosis. The dome interior has aerated-lung density, so its exact composition (aerated bowel, compressed lung, fluid) cannot be determined on projection radiography. Pretrained pathology classifiers (DenseNet, ResNet) gave low scores for atelectasis/effusion/mass/hernia and did not flag the finding; a community bone-fracture model behaved out-of-domain (flagged a blank image as fractured) and was discarded; view classification, the two anatomy segmentation models and the MedSAM delineation were in-domain and cross-validated. No prior images for comparison; upper abdomen partly cropped. Second-opinion support output; not a substitute for clinical correlation.

findings: Frontal (likely supine AP) chest radiograph of an adult. Large, homogeneous left basal/retrocardiac opacity with a smooth upper border running from the left heart border downward and laterally to the left lateral chest wall; the left hemidiaphragm and the medial left costophrenic angle are obscured and the left costophrenic region is opacified; the gastric bubble is visible below the opacity. No air bronchograms, no air-fluid level and no retrocardiac gas are seen. The left hemidiaphragm appears elevated relative to the right. The right hemidiaphragm is also elevated (supine position/hypoinflation) with a sharp right costophrenic angle and otherwise clear right lung base. The cardiac silhouette is not enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.24-0.30 measured above the opacity); the apparent cardiac prominence is due to the opacity fusing with the heart border. Trachea is midline and mediastinal contours are otherwise unremarkable. A nasogastric/orogastric tube is in place, crossing the diaphragm with its tip in the gastric region. No pneumothorax, no definite nodule or mass, and no rib or clavicle fracture are identified. External artifacts: dental restorations in the mandible, a metallic clip over the left lateral chest wall, and a faint external line over the right neck.
impression: Large left basal/retrocardiac opacity, most consistent with left lower lobe atelectasis, likely with an associated left pleural effusion; a layering left pleural effusion alone or an elevated left hemidiaphragm with gastric distension cannot be excluded on this single frontal view. No cardiomegaly. Nasogastric tube in appropriate position.
limitations: Single frontal view, likely supine AP: no lateral or decubitus view, so pleural effusion, atelectasis and diaphragmatic elevation cannot be definitively separated; AP projection magnifies the heart and mediastinum. 8-bit PNG export without DICOM metadata (no original windowing, no patient or technique data). Deep-learning outputs (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50, PSPNet, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM) were used only as corroborating evidence after flip/view/modality sanity checks; PSPNet diaphragm/heart classes and MedSAM masks proved unreliable in the presence of the opacity, and the automatic CTR was discarded. Subtle nodule-level findings cannot be excluded in an 8-bit rendering.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (likely portable AP, scapulae overlying the lung fields) with external ECG electrodes and multiple monitoring leads overlying the thorax. A patchy, ill-defined opacity occupies the right mid and lower lung zones, extending to the base; it is heterogeneous with internal aerated lucencies (air-bronchogram-like) and irregular borders, rather than a sharply marginated discrete mass. The right costophrenic angle is at least partly preserved, suggesting at most a trace or small effusion. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is within normal limits for a frontal projection and the trachea is midline. The left lung is comparatively clear. Two or three small metallic surgical clips are present below the left hemidiaphragm in the upper abdomen. A small, indeterminate metallic linear density is seen within the right lower zone opacity (possible tiny surgical clip or foreign body; uncertain). No pneumothorax, no definite rib fracture, and no indwelling chest tube or central venous catheter are identified; all linear structures appear to be external monitoring leads.
impression: Patchy right mid and lower zone consolidation, most consistent with pneumonia of the right middle/lower lobe, in a patient monitored with external ECG leads. A pulmonary mass with surrounding infiltrate is less likely but cannot be excluded on this single view; at most a trace right pleural effusion.
limitations: Single frontal view only, likely portable AP with scapular overlap and cardiac magnification; no lateral, decubitus, or prior comparison films, so effusion size and exact lobar localization are uncertain. Image is a digitized 8-bit PNG with reduced dynamic range. External ECG electrodes and lead wires overlie the right lung field and may mask or mimic pathology. Model-based evidence is supporting only: global non-localizing classifiers (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50, MIMIC-trained JF DenseNet) showed a present opacity with weak-to-moderate pneumonia/consolidation signal and no strong mass or cardiomegaly; a promptable segmenter failed to delineate a discrete mass (negative result); zero-shot BiomedCLIP was non-discriminative; out-of-domain models (pediatric-wrist YOLO and a bone-fracture classifier, the latter giving a strong false 'Fractured' positive) were rejected. The small metallic density in the right opacity is indeterminate.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Large right basilar opacity with a sharp, nearly horizontal superior margin at mid-thoracic level, homogeneous fluid density (no aerated lung below the margin), extending to the lateral chest wall and obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border, consistent with a large right pleural effusion with adjacent atelectasis/consolidation. Diffuse reticulonodular, mottled parenchymal opacities in the right upper and mid zones; milder mottling around the left hilum. A chest tube (pleural drain) is in situ in the left hemithorax, running from the left axilla down the lateral chest wall toward the left base. No definite pneumothorax: the thin oblique line in the left upper zone follows the course of the left oblique fissure, with no lucent zone devoid of lung markings. The left lung is otherwise aerated to the base; the left costophrenic angle is sharp; gastric air is seen below the left hemidiaphragm. The trachea appears near midline. An indeterminate corner bracket with two-letter text (a study/hospital label) is present in the top right corner.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with adjacent right basilar atelectasis/consolidation, and bilateral (right-predominant) mottled interstitial/alveolar opacities of indeterminate character; chest tube in situ in the left hemithorax; no definite pneumothorax. Single frontal view; etiologies of the effusion and parenchymal pattern cannot be determined from this image alone.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view, no prior comparison). Overpenetration reduces contrast in the lower zones; the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border are obscured, and tracheal/mediastinal position cannot be reliably quantified. The top-right marker is a non-standard label; orientation was inferred from the cardiac apex direction (normal). The character of the mottled opacities (infiltrate vs edema vs fibrosis) is indeterminate without clinical data. Pretrained outputs were supporting evidence only: DenseNet-121 (top score effusion) is concordant with the visual reading; PSPNet segmentation failed its sanity check on this image and was rejected; the zero-shot CLIP ranking (pneumothorax top) conflicted with the visual analysis and was not trusted; the pediatric wrist YOLO detector is out of domain and contributed no clinical information.

findings: Frontal (portable AP) chest radiograph. Extensive streaky subcutaneous emphysema, most marked in the right neck, axilla and lateral chest wall, with lesser involvement of the left lateral chest wall. The right hemithorax shows right lung volume loss (right lung area approximately half that of the left) with a lucent peripheral zone between the right lung and the lateral chest wall and a visible lateral lung margin, consistent with a right pneumothorax. No definite gross mediastinal or tracheal shift (trachea approximately midline). A non-specific hazy opacity is present in the left mid-to-lower lung zone. The right hemidiaphragm appears elevated. External ECG monitoring leads/electrodes are present; no definite chest drain is seen.
impression: Probable right pneumothorax with extensive right-predominant subcutaneous emphysema and right lung volume loss, without definite mediastinal shift (no tension physiology). A non-specific left mid-to-lower zone opacity is also present.
limitations: Portable AP projection with patient rotation and external monitoring devices; overall low contrast. Extensive superimposed subcutaneous emphysema overlaps the right pleural space, making it difficult to definitively separate pleural air (pneumothorax) from chest-wall gas - the pneumothorax is probable but not certain. Single frontal view only; no lateral or decubitus view to confirm pneumothorax or effusion. The left mid-to-lower zone opacity is non-specific without additional views or clinical context. Pretrained pathology models are out of distribution for this abnormal film, and their scores were used only as weak corroboration.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A hazy, ill-defined opacity is present in the left lower lung zone, denser medially (retrocardiac) and extending toward the left costophrenic angle; it obscures the left hemidiaphragm and the left heart border, and the left costophrenic angle is blunted (right costophrenic angle is sharp). The left lower zone is measurably denser than the contralateral zone (mean 128 vs 83 gray levels). No air bronchograms are identified within the opacity. The right lung is clear and well aerated. No pneumothorax. The trachea is midline and there is no mediastinal shift. Cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.44 (manual measurement, 0.42-0.46 accounting for the obscured left heart border), so the cardiac silhouette is not enlarged. No definite rib fracture or other skeletal abnormality is visible on direct inspection. A bright band along the inferior image edge is a table/detector artifact, not a finding.
impression: Left lower zone opacity with blunting of the left costophrenic angle, most consistent with a moderate left pleural effusion, likely with associated left lower lobe atelectasis or consolidation. No radiographic evidence of cardiomegaly, pneumothorax, or rib fracture.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral or decubitus): effusion versus consolidation versus atelectasis cannot be fully separated, and a subtle lateral meniscus cannot be confirmed or excluded. PA versus AP projection is unknown, which affects interpretation of the cardiothoracic ratio (a ratio of 0.44 would read slightly smaller if the view is PA). The left heart border is partially obscured by the opacity, adding +/-15 px uncertainty to the CT ratio. No clinical context (age, sex, symptoms) is available. A table/detector artifact band crosses the bottom of the image. The fracture-detection tools available in this environment are trained on wrist radiographs (out of domain) and were rejected, so skeletal assessment rests on direct visual inspection. Both available chest-structure segmentation models under-segmented the heart on this image, so the CT ratio was measured with manually verified landmarks.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (view classifier: Frontal, probability 0.996). Right pleural drainage catheter (chest tube) in situ: it enters the right hemithorax in the upper zone, its proximal segment is coiled in the right upper lung field, and the catheter descends along the right lateral chest wall with its tip curled at the right base. Moderate right lower-zone opacity with blunting/obscuration of the right costophrenic angle and obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm; the right lower lung zone is markedly denser than the corresponding left zone (zone medians 165 vs 124; see measurements/08_lung_zone_stats.csv) and anatomical segmentation classifies the right base as diaphragm rather than aerated lung. No pneumothorax is visible: pulmonary markings extend to the right chest wall, no pleural line is identified, and peripheral density is not more lucent than the left. Left lung field is clear with a sharp left costophrenic angle. Cardiac silhouette is not enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio 0.28). No rib fracture is identified. No other foreign device is present.
impression: Right-sided pleural drainage catheter in situ with a moderate right basal opacity, most consistent with a pleural effusion (partially drained/residual, with or without dependent atelectasis). No definite pneumothorax and no cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single frontal view only; PA vs AP and upright vs supine position are unknown, which affects assessment of effusion distribution and cardiac size; no lateral view. Image is an 8-bit PNG without original DICOM data (display-dependent contrast, no HU). The indwelling tube superimposes on the right lung field and demonstrably confounds some model outputs (DenseNet effusion and pneumothorax scores fall materially when the tube is inpainted; see measurements/05_classifier_tube_robustness.json). The 159-class anatomy segmentation model and the autoencoder anomaly map were unreliable on this image and were used only as documented negative results. Whole-image pathology classifiers are not side-specific and their calibrated thresholds are only approximate. Clinical context (reason for catheter, drainage output) is not available and was not inferred.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph. Dense opacification of the left mid and lower hemithorax, obscuring the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm; a hazy veil with residual aeration and visible vascular markings caps the left upper zone. The upper border of the dense opacity is oblique, higher medially (no laterally rising meniscus on this non-upright film). Slight contralateral (rightward) tracheal/mediastinal deviation, approximately 8-10 mm from the manubrium/clavicular midline. Right lung is aerated without focal consolidation or pneumothorax; right costophrenic angle preserved. Central venous catheter with a hub in the right infraclavicular region, the catheter coursing medially and inferiorly toward the SVC (tip not clearly identified); multiple ECG monitoring leads and electrodes overlie the chest. No definite rib fracture seen on the visualized right side; left posterior ribs are obscured by the opacity. Cardiac size not assessable (left border obscured, AP magnification).
impression: Large left pleural effusion with associated compressive atelectasis of the left lung and slight contralateral mediastinal shift, on a semi-erect/supine portable film. Left lung collapse (whiteout) is the main alternative but is less consistent with the contralateral tracheal deviation and the residual apical aeration.
limitations: Single AP portable view (semi-erect/supine) with probable mild rotation; no upright or lateral view to confirm a meniscus or fully characterize the collection; no prior for comparison. The dense left opacity obscures the left heart border, hilum and left ribs. Multiple external monitoring devices overlie the thorax and the catheter tip position is not clearly assessable. 8-bit image storage limits dynamic range. The 18-label computer-aided classifiers provide no laterality: the DenseNet output was judged out-of-distribution on this image (false-positive pneumothorax score) and not relied upon; the ResNet output was weak and used only as a soft supporting signal; the BiomedCLIP collapse-vs-effusion ordering conflicts with the measured tracheal geometry and was not relied upon; fracture detectors were out of domain for a chest radiograph. The tracheal deviation is small, so the direction of shift is a borderline finding.

findings: Frontal (AP) chest radiograph with external ECG electrodes and leads overlying the chest. Mild, bilateral, fairly symmetric interstitial/reticular markings in the mid and lower lung zones with prominent pulmonary vessels; no focal dense consolidation, no definite pneumothorax, and no large pleural effusion identified. The lower lung zones, diaphragmatic detail, and costophrenic angles are partially obscured by a bright, homogeneous upper-abdominal/diaphragmatic region (liver and bowel gas), which is anatomical rather than a pathological opacity. The cardiac silhouette appears moderately prominent but is magnified by the AP projection and its lower border is obscured, so heart size is not confidently assessed. No definite fracture is seen in the visualized clavicles, proximal humeri, or ribs.
impression: Technically limited frontal chest radiograph showing a mild, non-specific bilateral interstitial pattern with prominent pulmonary vessels and no definite acute focal abnormality. The interstitial pattern is most consistent with early/mild interstitial pulmonary edema in this inpatient context, with chronic interstitial change or atypical infection as alternatives.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) view with no lateral; overall low contrast / washed-out image; bright upper-abdominal region obscures the lower lung zones, diaphragm, and costophrenic angles; external ECG electrodes and leads overlie the chest; AP projection magnifies the heart and limits cardiac size assessment; pretrained model scores were weak and inconsistent (several were shown to reflect model priors rather than image signal, and the segmentation-based cardiothoracic ratio was unreliable), so AI support for any specific diagnosis is limited.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (AP projection). Multiple small metallic surgical clips (approximately 12 to 13) are present in the right upper hemithorax and right axilla, consistent with prior surgery (for example breast or axillary surgery). The lungs are well aerated bilaterally; no definite consolidation, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, or pulmonary edema is seen. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is unremarkable and the heart size is normal (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.35). The right hemidiaphragm is slightly higher than the left (approximately 1.4 cm), which is within the normal range, with a smooth contour. The bony thorax appears intact with no acute fracture identified. Note: two independent pretrained classifiers both assign a high probability to 'hernia', but no definite retrocardiac opacity or air-fluid level is visible on inspection, and the left base is hazy due to overexposure.
impression: Frontal chest radiograph showing incidental multiple surgical clips in the right upper hemithorax/axilla (consistent with prior breast or axillary surgery) and no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. The lungs are clear and the heart size is normal. A possible subtle hiatal hernia is suggested by the models but not visually confirmed.
limitations: Single frontal (likely AP) view only; no lateral or decubitus view to exclude a small pleural effusion, retrocardiac pathology, or posterior atelectasis. The image is an 8-bit PNG (not DICOM) with fixed windowing, and the central and lower regions are washed out/overexposed, limiting evaluation of the right heart border, the left hemidiaphragm, and the retrocardiac region; the cardiothoracic ratio and left dome height are therefore estimates. Pretrained model scores are calibrated probabilities, not diagnoses: the high 'hernia' score from two models could not be visually corroborated and is not reported as a finding, and out-of-domain models (a pediatric wrist detector and a community fracture classifier) were run and correctly excluded. The exact relationship of the surgical clips to the lung parenchyma versus the chest wall cannot be determined from a single projection.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (L marker; confirmed frontal by view classifier, 0.996). The right hemidiaphragm is markedly elevated: smooth, thin, continuous dome-shaped border with lung markings extending to it and a sharp right costophrenic angle (no effusion); the dome apex lies at approximately the 8th-9th posterior rib (segmentation model numbering: 9th-10th), about 1-2 rib intervals higher than the left hemidiaphragm, which also sits lower than its usual 7th-8th posterior rib position (dome apex ~9th-10th posterior rib). A well-defined round soft-tissue opacity (~90-110 px in image coordinates) projects left of the spine at the lower cardiac level, above the diaphragm, in the expected position of the esophageal hiatus, without a definite air-fluid level. Mild hazy density in the right lower zone above the dome, consistent with minor basilar atelectasis. Heart size normal (segmentation-based cardiothoracic ratio ~0.44). Trachea midline, mediastinum unremarkable. Lungs otherwise clear: no consolidation, no definite nodule (a few tiny dot-like densities in the right mid-zone are indeterminate, likely vessels on end), no pneumothorax. Clavicles and ribs intact, no fracture. A thin curvilinear line along the left lateral chest wall is a skin-fold artifact. The upper abdomen shows a prominent gas pattern (gastric bubble, mottled colonic gas).
impression: Elevated right hemidiaphragm (dominant finding), with the left hemidiaphragm also low-positioned, and a round retrocardiac opacity most consistent with a hiatal hernia; no acute cardiopulmonary process identified.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral to separate the retrocardiac opacity from pericardial fat or to confirm an air-fluid level); cropped field of view (lateral chest walls, shoulders, lower abdomen cut off); absolute rib level of the domes carries ~1-2 rib uncertainty between manual counting and the segmentation model (right dome 8th-9th vs 9th-10th posterior rib); the hiatal-hernia diagnosis is supported by morphology plus two concordant CNN classifiers (raw sigmoids 0.99 and 0.79) but not proven - a third model (NIH-only weights) disagreed and CT would be needed to confirm; small dot-like opacities in the right mid-zone are indeterminate (vessels vs tiny nodules); zero-shot vision-language scoring was uninformative and out-of-domain fracture models were unreliable, so neither was used.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph, adequately penetrated and positioned. Lungs are well aerated without definite consolidation, mass, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax; costophrenic angles are sharp. Cardiomediastinal silhouette is within normal limits (measured cardiothoracic ratio ~0.39) and the trachea is midline. The bony thorax is intact without acute fracture. Two subtle findings: (1) a subtle, ill-defined oval soft-tissue density in the peripheral right mid-lung zone, roughly 1.5-2 cm, denser than the adjacent aerated lung; a superimposition of chest wall/rib or a nipple shadow is favored, but a small pulmonary nodule cannot be excluded on this single view; (2) mild streaky opacity at the right lung base consistent with linear (plate-like) atelectasis, with slightly increased right basilar density.
impression: Mostly normal frontal chest radiograph without definite acute cardiopulmonary disease. Minor incidental findings only: mild right basilar atelectasis and a subtle, ill-defined right mid-lung opacity (superimposition or nipple shadow favored, small nodule not excluded). If there is any clinical concern, correlation with prior imaging or an additional lateral/oblique view is recommended to characterize the right mid-lung opacity.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral), so the subtle right mid-lung opacity cannot be localized or characterized (superimposition vs parenchymal). Dark corner/detector-edge artifacts at the top of the image slightly limit the extreme apices. Pretrained pathology classifiers (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50) returned weak, non-specific signals near their population operating thresholds and were used only as supporting cross-checks; two provided detectors (a pediatric-wrist YOLO and a community bone-fracture model) are out of domain for a chest radiograph and returned untrustworthy outputs, so they were not used to support any finding. No clinical context, patient demographics, or prior images were available.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. An implantable venous access port (port-a-cath) is present in the right upper chest, with an attached catheter that courses superiorly then medially and inferiorly into the region of the superior vena cava, consistent with an appropriately positioned right-sided central venous port. Both lungs are well-aerated without focal consolidation, mass, or definite nodule; no pleural effusion or pneumothorax. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size and contour and the trachea is midline. Normal gastric air bubble and colonic gas are seen; no definite free intraperitoneal air. No definite acute osseous abnormality. A thin linear density and two small metallic-appearing objects are noted in the lower abdomen (indeterminate; likely external artifact or surgical clips).
impression: Frontal chest radiograph showing a right-sided implantable venous access port (port-a-cath) with an appropriately positioned catheter. No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality is identified (no consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax, or cardiomegaly). The implanted port is the dominant finding.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral), limiting finding localization and assessment of pneumothorax and the mediastinum. The port and catheter produce superimposition/artifact over the right mid-lung. Pretrained chest segmentation (PSPNet) was unreliable on this image, so no segmentation-derived measurements were used; the implanted port is atypical for the pathology-classifier training data, so model scores are supporting evidence only. Small metallic-appearing objects and a linear density in the lower abdomen are indeterminate and not well characterized on a chest film. The exact catheter tip position is best confirmed on a dedicated view.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (AP projection, patient rotated, ICU setting) of a post-sternotomy patient (midline sternal wires). A left pigtail pleural drainage catheter is coiled in the left lower hemithorax. A thin catheter courses through the right hemithorax (identity and tip not fully evaluable), a ring-shaped metallic object lies in the right neck paramedian to the tracheal midline (most likely external artifact), and multiple external ECG electrodes overlay the chest. No endotracheal or tracheostomy tube is seen in the tracheal air column. Bilateral basal opacities: dense right lower zone opacity obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle, and hazy left lower zone opacity with a blunted left costophrenic angle (model-free intensity profile: lower vs upper zone mean intensity 178 vs 116 on the right, 152 vs 99 on the left), consistent with bilateral pleural effusions (right greater) with adjacent atelectasis and/or consolidation. Patchy mid-zone opacities are present bilaterally. No pneumothorax (apical lung markings reach the chest wall bilaterally). Heart size cannot be reliably assessed on this AP film with obscured borders.
impression: Post-sternotomy ICU chest radiograph showing bilateral pleural effusions (right > left) with bilateral lower-zone opacities (atelectasis vs consolidation vs mild pulmonary edema not separable on a single AP view), a left pigtail pleural catheter in situ, no pneumothorax, and multiple lines and external devices. Most consistent with postoperative fluid overload/effusions with adjacent atelectasis; multifocal pneumonia or aspiration cannot be excluded.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) view without a lateral; patient rotation and supine/ICU positioning limit quantification of effusion size and assessment of mediastinal width; numerous overlapping lines, tubes and external devices obscure parts of the lungs and make some catheter tips and the right-neck ring-shaped object indeterminate; heart size is unreliable on an AP film; PNG export without DICOM metadata (no kVp, projection or patient data). Pretrained model outputs were only partially trustworthy on this image (DenseNet scores collapsed to a flat ~0.5 band; PSPNet segmentation failed over the effused zones; BiomedCLIP zero-shot ranked 'normal' highest; ResNet scores shift under left-right mirroring) and were used only to corroborate findings directly visible in the original image.

findings: Supine anteroposterior portable chest radiograph. Bilateral diffuse alveolar and interstitial opacities, more confluent in the right mid and lower zones (right greater than left) and in the dependent zones of both lungs, with perihilar predominance; no air bronchograms and no pneumothorax identified. Lower zones are hazy and the costophrenic angles are not sharply seen, raising the possibility of small bilateral pleural effusions that cannot be excluded in the supine position. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent, but the degree of cardiomegaly cannot be assessed on a supine AP film. A large, smooth, homogeneous, dome-shaped opacity over the right lower hemithorax, with ribs visible through it and no spiculation or meniscus, is a breast shadow (external soft tissue), confirmed as a discrete well-circumscribed structure on promptable segmentation. Lines and devices: a right-sided central venous catheter with a plausible course toward the SVC (tip not sharply resolved); a midline tube running from the neck through the chest into the upper abdomen (enteric tube; an endotracheal tube, if present, cannot be confirmed on this single view); a left-sided line of uncertain identity; multiple ECG electrodes and monitoring cables; an external device on the left chest wall; and a safety-pin-like metallic external object over the mid chest. No definite rib fracture is identified.
impression: Bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities in a monitored, critically ill patient, most consistent with pulmonary edema or ARDS with a dependent, perihilar pattern; multifocal pneumonia is also possible and cannot be separated from edema on this single supine film. Probable small bilateral pleural effusions. Apparent cardiomegaly is unconfirmed (supine AP magnification). A right breast shadow and multiple support lines and external devices limit evaluation. No definite focal mass, pneumothorax, or fracture.
limitations: Single supine AP portable view: effusions layer posteriorly, the cardiac silhouette is magnified, and the diaphragm is elevated, so cardiomegaly and effusion size cannot be quantified; no lateral view or prior study for comparison. Numerous external lines, electrodes, and a left chest-wall device overlie the lungs, and a right breast shadow obscures part of the right lower zone. The right-sided catheter tip and the presence/tip of an endotracheal tube cannot be confidently assessed. Pretrained pathology classifiers were mostly trained on conventional (often erect) chest radiograph datasets and disagree on etiology (edema vs pneumonia), so the etiology remains indeterminate; PSPNet anatomical segmentation was unreliable on this image and was not used for measurements; no clinical context is available.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. There is a hazy opacity in the left lower lung zone with blunting/obscuration of the left costophrenic angle and a slightly concave (meniscus-like) upper margin, most consistent with a left pleural effusion with associated left lower-lobe atelectasis. Multiple tubes/lines are present: a tubular catheter along the left lateral chest wall (in keeping with a left chest drain), a looped catheter at the right lower chest wall/flank, and thin external monitoring leads overlying the right hemithorax. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent (manual cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.53), but its inferior and left borders are obscured by the overexposed lower field and the left basal opacity. The right lung is well aerated and clear; there is no pneumothorax and no overt pulmonary edema.
impression: Left pleural effusion with associated left lower-lobe atelectasis, in a patient with a left chest drain in situ. The cardiac silhouette is borderline enlarged, but the degree of cardiomegaly is uncertain. No pneumothorax or pulmonary edema.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral). The lower field is overexposed, obscuring the inferior heart border, the diaphragms, and the left heart border; the left heart border is additionally obscured by the left basal opacity, so the cardiothoracic ratio (approx 0.53) is an uncertain estimate. Projection (PA vs AP) is unknown, which affects heart size. Pretrained model outputs (pathology classifiers, segmentation, zero-shot CLIP) are supportive but not definitive: the two pathology classifiers disagreed on cardiomegaly, PSPNet under-segmented the heart, and image-level scores are perturbed by the overlying tubes/lines and the bright field. The identities and courses of the tubes cannot be fully determined on a single frontal film.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of a monitored patient (multiple ECG electrodes and external lead wires; a cylindrical external device lies beside the patient's right forearm, outside the body contour, indicated by the arrow). There is a large right-sided airspace opacity: a patchy, hazy process in the right mid zone overlying a dense, confluent basal opacity that obscures the right hemidiaphragm and the right heart border; the right costophrenic angle is not visible and the upper border of the opacity is higher medially than laterally. The left lung is aerated and essentially clear with a sharp left costophrenic angle; the apparent left basal density matches hemidiaphragm superimposition. No pleural line or avascular space is identified, i.e., no visible pneumothorax. A midline enteric tube (nasogastric tube) descends in a normal, non-coiled course; its tip is not definitively visualized below the diaphragm. Multiple short linear metallic densities (including a V-shaped clip-like structure) are present in a left paraspinal band from the upper mediastinum to the upper abdomen, most consistent with surgical clips; uncertain significance. The trachea is midline; no definite rib or clavicular fracture is seen.
impression: Right lower zone consolidation (pneumonia) with associated right pleural effusion in a monitored patient, with an enteric tube in normal visible course; left lung clear; no visible pneumothorax.
limitations: Single portable AP (likely supine/semi-erect) view without a lateral view: the cardiac silhouette is not reliably measurable (right heart border obscured by the adjacent opacity, AP magnification), and small anterior pneumothoraces or small effusions can be missed. Assessment of the right base is degraded by superimposition of the adducted right arm, an ECG electrode and external cables. The image is a windowed 8-bit PNG (not DICOM), so absolute densities are non-standard; quantitative ROI comparisons are valid only within this image. The enteric tube tip is not definitively identified below the diaphragm. Pretrained model outputs (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50, BiomedCLIP) were used only as corroborating evidence: this AP portable film with heavy device overlap is atypical of their training data, the PSPNet segmentation masks proved unreliable here and were discarded for quantification, and an uncorroborated 'mass' signal from one classifier was excluded. The significance of the metallic densities cannot be determined without clinical history.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (AP or PA projection), single view. Both lungs are well aerated overall, with mild bilateral perihilar and lower-zone reticular interstitial prominence. No definite focal consolidation, no air bronchograms, no pleural effusion (costophrenic angles sharp), and no pneumothorax. Cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size and contour (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.44 by intensity-based measurement). Trachea is midline; hila are not enlarged; mediastinum is not widened. Osseous structures (ribs, clavicles, scapulae, proximal humeri) appear intact with no definite fracture. External radiopaque lead marker over the left shoulder region (patient's left).
impression: No definite acute intrathoracic abnormality. Mild bilateral interstitial prominence, which may be a normal variant or an early/mild lower respiratory infection in a symptomatic patient; clinical correlation is advised.
limitations: Single frontal projection without lateral view; 8-bit image with black borders and the detector field cropped at the image edge; no patient age, sex or clinical history available (the patient could be a child or a small adult, which limits the applicability of adult-trained classifiers). Segmentation models (PSPNet, UNetResNet50) behaved out of domain on this image and were rejected for measurements; classifier scores (DenseNet121, ResNet50) are uncalibrated and were used only as directional cross-checks; the cardiothoracic ratio is an approximate intensity-based measurement; a subtle basilar opacity cannot be fully excluded.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (AP-type projection). A pigtail drainage catheter is present in the right hemithorax, entering the right lateral chest wall with its tip coiled at the right apex. There is a right apical/lateral pneumothorax: an air-density, avascular band between the right chest wall and the lung edge, with a faint pleural line at the lung margin; the left lung reaches the chest wall at the same level. Subcutaneous emphysema is present, most prominent as streaky gas in the right axillary/lateral chest wall and flank soft tissues, with milder involvement of the neck/supraclavicular regions. Diffuse bilateral reticular and patchy alveolar opacities are seen, more prominent in the right mid and upper zones. Two rounded opacities are present in the left lung: a larger (approximately 3-4 cm), somewhat ill-defined opacity in the left lower zone just above the hemidiaphragm, and a smaller (approximately 2 cm) round opacity in the left upper zone; both are nodule/mass-suspect. The cardiac silhouette is normal in size, the trachea is midline, no definite pleural effusion is seen, and no definite rib fracture is identified.
impression: Right pneumothorax with subcutaneous emphysema and a pigtail drainage catheter in situ, on a background of diffuse bilateral interstitial/alveolar opacities and left-lung nodule(s). The acute findings (pneumothorax, emphysema, catheter) are the dominant abnormalities.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view), so pneumothorax extent and nodule characterization are approximate. Image is an 8-bit rescaled PNG without original DICOM HU data, so air and soft-tissue densities are compressed and the pleural line is faint. Likely portable AP geometry may magnify the cardiac silhouette and degrade lateral detail. Pretrained model support was partial and discordant: the xrv ResNet-512 model strongly favored pneumothorax/emphysema while the xrv DenseNet-224 model was neutral on those labels (both agreed on a nodular process); PSPNet segmentation and the ResNet autoencoder reconstruction error were unhelpful at the needed resolution and were discarded; the pediatric-wrist YOLO detector and the community bone-fracture classifier are out of domain and were rejected. No clinical history or prior imaging is available.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. There is a hazy, ill-defined opacity in the left mid-lung zone centred on the left hilum/lingula, and a rounded, fairly well-circumscribed soft-tissue opacity (approximately 1-2 cm) in the left lower lung zone (nodule/mass). The right lung is relatively well-aerated without definite focal consolidation. Both costophrenic angles are sharp, with no pleural effusion. No pneumothorax. The cardiac silhouette is not clearly enlarged, although the cardiomediastinal contour is mildly prominent (may reflect AP projection magnification). No definite rib or clavicle fracture. A radiopaque 'L' side marker is present over the left shoulder. Breast shadows overlie the lower lung fields.
impression: Left lung abnormality: a rounded left lower-zone opacity (nodule/mass) together with a hazy left perihilar/mid-zone opacity. The rounded opacity is the most definite finding. The right lung is clear, with no effusion or pneumothorax.
limitations: Single frontal (likely AP) view; no lateral and no prior for comparison. Low image contrast with noise, and breast shadows partially obscure the lower lung fields. Image-level CNN classifiers provide no localisation and disagree on the degree of parenchymal infiltrate (DenseNet borderline-positive, ResNet essentially negative); zero-shot BiomedCLIP similarity is not calibrated. PSPNet segmentation was low quality (heart under-segmented, left-lung mask leaked into the chest wall), so its quantitative lung-zone opacities and cardiothoracic ratio are unreliable.
