limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection limits assessment of posterior vs anterior pathology. Overlying medical devices (central line, ECG leads, catheter tubing) obscure portions of both lung fields and may produce artifacts. Pretrained classifiers showed divergent results (DenseNet121 with high baseline activation vs ResNet50 with conservative scoring), limiting their reliability. PSPNet segmentation at 512x512 resolution from center-cropped input loses peripheral detail. No CT correlation available. Cardiac silhouette assessment limited by adjacent opacity.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph showing multiple medical devices including tracheostomy tube, right chest tube(s), central venous catheter from left subclavian region, and ECG monitoring leads. Dense, confluent opacity occupies the right upper lung zone with near-complete opacification. Patchy, hazy opacity in the right lower lung zone with obscured right hemidiaphragm and blunted costophrenic angle. Diffuse, patchy bilateral infiltrates present in the left lung field, less dense than right-sided findings. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged, though AP portable projection magnifies the heart. Multiple radiopaque lines and tubes traverse the chest, limiting full assessment of underlying anatomy.
impression: Extensive right-sided pulmonary opacity with dense upper zone component and hazy lower zone component, consistent with consolidation and pleural effusion. Bilateral infiltrates present with right-sided predominance. Clinical context of ICU patient with tracheostomy and chest drainage. Findings are most consistent with multifocal pneumonia with right-sided pleural effusion, though pulmonary edema and ARDS remain in the differential.
limitations: AP portable projection with patient rotation magnifies cardiac silhouette and reduces spatial resolution. Heavy medical device overlay (tracheostomy tube, chest tubes, central line, ECG leads) obscures underlying anatomy and limits assessment of lung parenchyma. Single-view imaging prevents evaluation of depth and posterior structures. Pretrained models (DenseNet, ResNet, PSPNet) provided unreliable outputs due to out-of-distribution features (devices, AP view, heavy pathology). Bounding boxes are approximate due to ill-defined opacity margins. No lateral view available to assess effusion volume or posterior consolidation.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph demonstrates a left pneumothorax with a visible visceral pleural line. Two left-sided chest tubes are in place. A right-sided PICC line is present with its tip projecting over the superior vena cava. There is left lower lobe atelectasis. The right lung is clear. No definite rib fractures are visualized.
impression: Left pneumothorax with chest tubes in situ. Left basal atelectasis. Right PICC line in appropriate position.
limitations: Single frontal view limits 3D assessment. 8-bit PNG format with narrow intensity range (0-216) prevented reliable use of pretrained classifiers which produced non-discriminative outputs. Pretrained segmentation models also performed poorly. Small pneumothorax components may be missed. Medical devices (chest tubes, PICC line) may obscure underlying lung parenchyma.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph demonstrates extensive opacity in the right lower lung zone with obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border, consistent with consolidation and/or pleural effusion. A focal patchy opacity is present in the left mid-lung zone, corresponding to the location indicated by the annotation arrow. A central venous catheter is seen entering from the right neck region and coursing inferiorly through the superior vena cava. The cardiac silhouette appears widened but assessment is limited by AP projection. The right costophrenic angle is obscured.
impression: Right lower zone opacity with obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border, most consistent with right lower lobe consolidation with associated pleural effusion. Left mid-lung zone focal opacity at the arrow-indicated location. These findings are most suggestive of multifocal pneumonia. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged but assessment limited by portable AP projection.
limitations: Portable AP projection limits assessment of cardiac size and mediastinal contours. Single view without lateral projection prevents full characterization of findings. Supine or semi-supine positioning may affect fluid distribution. DenseNet classifier outputs are elevated for multiple pathologies likely due to normalization artifacts. PSPNet segmentation was inaccurate for this image type. No prior imaging available for comparison.

findings: Portable supine AP chest radiograph. Bilateral mid and lower zone opacities, more prominent and dense in the left lower zone (retrocardiac region), where the opacity obscures the left heart border and left hemidiaphragm consistent with consolidation. The right lower zone demonstrates patchy, less dense opacity consistent with atelectasis or early consolidation. The cardiac silhouette appears widened but assessment is limited by AP supine projection. ECG monitoring leads overlie the chest. A central venous catheter enters from the left upper chest with tip projecting over the superior vena cava. No definite pneumothorax identified on this supine view. Lung volumes appear reduced.
impression: Bilateral mid and lower zone airspace opacities, most prominent in the left retrocardiac region, in a patient with supportive devices in situ. The pattern is consistent with multifocal pneumonia or pulmonary edema. Left pleural effusion cannot be excluded on this supine view.
limitations: Single portable AP supine view limits assessment of cardiac size, pleural effusions, and subtle findings. Supine position causes fluid to layer posteriorly, potentially masking effusions. Overlying ECG monitoring leads and external wires create artifacts. Limited inspiratory effort reduces lung volume assessment. No lateral or upright views available for comparison. DenseNet classifier trained on diverse projections shows uniformly elevated scores for portable supine images, reducing discriminative value. PSPNet segmentation is unreliable for this image type.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph with multiple monitoring leads and a right-sided central venous catheter. Patchy, linear opacities are present in both lung bases, more prominent on the left, obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and left heart border. The upper lung fields are clear. No pneumothorax. The cardiac silhouette appears not significantly enlarged, though assessment is limited by AP projection. Low lung volumes are noted.
impression: Bibasilar atelectasis, more pronounced on the left, in the setting of low lung volumes on portable AP radiograph. Findings are most consistent with subsegmental atelectasis rather than consolidation or pleural effusion.
limitations: AP portable projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette and limits cardiac size assessment. Low lung volumes limit full lung field evaluation. Overlying ECG leads and monitoring cables may obscure subtle findings. Single frontal view without lateral makes it difficult to differentiate retrocardiac atelectasis from effusion. DenseNet121 classification was unreliable (all 18 pathologies positive) and not used for findings.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph of a patient with multiple indwelling medical devices including a right-sided chest tube with coiled proximal portion in the right upper lung, ECG monitoring leads, and external safety pin over the left axilla. There is a large right-sided pneumothorax with a visible visceral pleural line and absence of peripheral lung markings in the right upper to mid lung zones. The right chest tube is in situ. The left lower lung zone demonstrates a hazy opacity with associated volume loss, obscuring the left heart border. The left hemidiaphragm is elevated with a prominent gastric air bubble beneath it. Multiple bowel gas loops are visible in the upper abdomen.
impression: Right-sided pneumothorax with chest tube in situ. Left lower lobe opacity suggestive of atelectasis with possible superimposed consolidation or small effusion. The pneumothorax appears moderate in size despite the chest tube being in place.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection limits assessment of anterior vs posterior pneumothorax and precise effusion quantification. Multiple indwelling devices (chest tube, ECG leads, safety pin) create artifacts that obscure underlying anatomy. The DenseNet classifier produced uniformly elevated scores across all pathologies, indicating the image falls outside the model's training distribution due to extensive medical hardware, and its output could not be trusted for specific findings. Preprocessing normalization warning further reduced confidence in automated classification. Patient positioning appears non-standard. Abdominal contents are within the field of view, suggesting a portable AP projection.

findings: AP supine portable chest radiograph of a critically ill patient with extensive monitoring equipment including endotracheal tube, central venous catheters, chest tube on the right, nasogastric tube, and ECG leads. Marked airspace opacity involving the right mid and lower lung zones with obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle. Subtle retrocardiac and left lower zone opacity. Cardiac silhouette appears enlarged though assessment is limited by AP supine projection. No definitive pneumothorax identified, though assessment is limited by supine technique and overlying devices.
impression: Right mid and lower zone consolidation with probable associated pleural effusion, concerning for pneumonia. Left retrocardiac opacity may represent atelectasis or consolidation. Critically ill patient with multiple indwelling devices.
limitations: AP supine portable technique with extensive overlying medical devices significantly limits assessment. Supine positioning prevents meniscus visualization for pleural effusion evaluation. Cardiac silhouette magnified by AP projection, precluding reliable cardiomegaly assessment. Right lateral edge partially obscured by black artifact bar. Model outputs (DenseNet, PSPNet) trained on cleaner PA erect images may not fully generalize to this portable study with numerous devices.

findings: Large right-sided pleural effusion with meniscus sign, occupying the right mid-to-lower hemithorax and obscuring the right heart border, right hemidiaphragm, and right costophrenic angle. Smaller left pleural effusion with blunting of the left costophrenic angle. Enlarged cardiac silhouette with mediastinal shift to the left. Expiration-phase film as indicated by radiographic marker. Overlying right lower lobe atelectasis/consolidation cannot be excluded.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift to the left, smaller left pleural effusion, and cardiomegaly. The dominant finding is the right-sided pleural effusion which accounts for the extensive right hemithorax opacity.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral projection limits depth localization and cardiac assessment. Expiration-phase film reduces lung volumes and may exaggerate vascular markings. Right heart border and hemidiaphragm are obscured by effusion, preventing assessment of underlying consolidation. PSPNet segmentation unreliable due to extensive pathology. BiomedCLIP scores non-discriminative. DenseNet121 may produce false positives for Mass, Fibrosis, and Nodule due to large opacity.

findings: Moderate to large right pleural effusion with meniscus sign, occupying the lower right hemithorax. Right mid-zone patchy opacity consistent with consolidation and/or compressive atelectasis above the effusion. Small left pleural effusion with blunting of the left costophrenic angle. The right heart border is obscured by the right-sided opacity. External ECG monitoring leads and a tubular structure (possibly a catheter or chest tube) are visible overlying the right chest wall. The left lung field is otherwise clear.
impression: Right-sided pleural effusion with associated compressive atelectasis or consolidation in the right mid-zone, and a small contralateral (left) pleural effusion. The findings are consistent with bilateral pleural disease, with the right side being predominantly affected. Differential includes parapneumonic effusion, malignant effusion, or transudative effusion from heart failure.
limitations: Single frontal view only; no lateral projection available to confirm posterior extent of effusions. The right heart border is obscured, preventing accurate cardiac size assessment. External monitoring leads and possible catheter overlie the right chest wall, potentially obscuring underlying structures. DenseNet model provides classification but not spatial localization; PSPNet segmentation is trained on normal chest X-rays and may not accurately segment pathological regions. The left effusion is small and could be artifactual or represent pleural thickening rather than free fluid.

findings: Frontal (AP) chest radiograph of a pediatric patient. A focal, somewhat confluent hazy opacity is present in the right mid-to-lower zone (right middle/lower lobe region), with a thin linear structure traversing it that may be a displaced minor fissure; a confluent core is centered over the right mid zone. The left lung shows diffuse peribronchial/basal hazy markings (peribronchial thickening) that are overall hazier than the right. The cardiac silhouette is not enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.26-0.30); mediastinum is midline; hila are not enlarged. No pleural effusion (both costophrenic angles sharp) and no pneumothorax. No rib fracture. An external thin radiopaque monitoring lead crosses the right chest wall from the right axilla to the lower midline (visible outside the body silhouette, so external, not a catheter). A sharply marginated radiopaque device projects over the left shoulder, external to the thorax.
impression: Focal right mid-to-lower zone pulmonary opacity (consolidation/infiltrate) with diffuse peribronchial changes, most consistent with pneumonia in a monitored pediatric patient.
limitations: Single frontal (AP) view only, no lateral; pediatric AP geometry magnifies the cardiac silhouette and overlaps anatomy. External monitoring lead over the right chest and a metallic device over the left shoulder (both external) can obscure adjacent lung and mimic pathology. PSPNet anatomical segmentation was unreliable on this image and was not used quantitatively. Classifier and zero-shot model scores are secondary reads on a partially out-of-domain (pediatric, with artifacts) image and were used only to corroborate, not to establish, the opacity. Exact right middle vs lower lobe attribution is not possible on a single frontal view.

findings: Frontal (AP) chest radiograph of a monitored patient with a midline, appropriately positioned tracheostomy tube and external ECG electrodes. Low lung volumes with elevated right hemidiaphragm. Patchy air-space and reticular opacity in the right mid and lower zones overlying the elevated right hemidiaphragm, with the right costophrenic angle obscured. Confluent opacity in the left lower zone (retrocardiac) obscuring the left hemidiaphragm and left costophrenic angle, with patchy extension into the left mid-lower zone. Mild interstitial prominence in the mid zones. Cardiac silhouette not enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio 0.36 on structural segmentation). No pneumothorax. No discrete focal mass or nodule identified.
impression: Bilateral basilar opacities in a patient with low lung volumes, most consistent with basilar atelectasis and/or pneumonia, possibly accompanied by small bilateral pleural effusions (left greater than right). Portable AP technique and low lung volumes limit full assessment.
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral film); portable AP technique with cardiac magnification; low lung volumes; overlying ECG electrodes and lead wires; 8-bit re-exported image with reduced dynamic range (max 225 of 255); no prior studies for comparison; effusion, atelectasis and consolidation cannot be fully separated without a lateral view or ultrasound; cardiac silhouette assessment limited by adjacent opacities and projection.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. An indwelling device complex is present in the right hemithorax: a triangular plate-like radiopaque object (soft-tissue density) with two small lateral suture tabs projects over the right mid lung zone (right 5th-7th rib level); a thin catheter/lead attaches to its apex, ascends to a loop in the right brachiocephalic/subclavian region and then descends vertically along the right mediastinum, fading at approximately T6-T7 level. Inferolateral to the plate, a cluster of three small rounded opacities of bone-like density (each about 15-35 px, mottled interiors) projects over the right lower lung zone. Both lungs are otherwise clear: no consolidation, no pleural effusion (costophrenic angles sharp bilaterally), no pneumothorax (lung markings extend to the periphery at both apices). Cardiac silhouette is top-normal in size (measured cardiothoracic ratio about 0.51). Mediastinum not widened. No acute rib, clavicle or scapula fracture. A small compact round opacity (about 30 px) lies adjacent to the right mediastinal border, most consistent with an end-on pulmonary vessel; a ring-like lucency in the left mid zone corresponds to an end-on bronchus. Visualized upper abdomen unremarkable (normal gastric bubble).
impression: Implanted venous access device (port-like body with catheter) in the right hemithorax, with a cluster of three small dense (possibly calcified or device-fragment) round opacities in the right lower zone; no acute cardiopulmonary abnormality (no consolidation, effusion, pneumothorax or cardiomegaly).
limitations: Single frontal projection without lateral view: anterior-posterior position of the device and its relation to lung vs chest wall cannot be determined, and the device's exact identity requires clinical history or a second projection. The image is a 1024x1024 centered square crop that partially truncates the lateral chest walls. Pretrained classifiers have no device class, and their mild 'nodule/infiltration' scores may reflect the superimposed device; the MIMIC-specific DenseNet weights returned no usable labels in this build (uniform 0.5 scores). The small right paraspinal round opacity and the left mid-zone ring were evaluated and judged non-specific (end-on vessel / end-on bronchus) rather than lesions. CTR was measured by threshold-based border tracing on one view (uncertainty about +/-0.02).

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (appears pediatric/adolescent) showing a smooth, dome-shaped soft-tissue opacity in the left lower hemithorax whose apex reaches approximately the mid-thoracic level, about 69 px (~1.5 intercostal spaces) higher than the right hemidiaphragm at the midclavicular line. The gastric bubble lies below the dome at a normal abdominal level, the lung above the dome is aerated, and no air bronchograms are seen within the opacity. Mild leftward tracheal deviation at the carinal level, reduced vertical extent of the left lung field above the dome (~12% shorter than the right), and slightly narrowed upper-left intercostal spaces (~9%). The right lung is clear, the right costophrenic angle is sharp, and there is no pneumothorax, no definite effusion, and no consolidation elsewhere. The cardiac silhouette is displaced leftward and merged with the dome; heart size is not reliably assessable on this projection. Two small metallic surgical clips are present in the left upper quadrant adjacent to the gastric bubble. Mild mid-thoracic spinal curvature. No rib, clavicular, or scapular fractures identified.
impression: Elevated left hemidiaphragm (eventration pattern) producing a left basilar dome-shaped opacity with mild leftward mediastinal shift and mild ipsilateral volume loss; a component of left lower lobe atelectasis may be contributing.
limitations: Single AP frontal projection with no lateral view, so an elevated diaphragm cannot be definitively separated from adjacent left lower lobe collapse or a retrocardiac hernia; no prior imaging for comparison; apparent pediatric body habitus limits calibration of adult-trained classifier thresholds; heart size indeterminate due to displacement and projection; a small surgical clip implies prior surgery but history cannot be verified; all model-based outputs were used only as cross-checks after domain and sanity verification.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of a monitored/acute-care patient. Diffuse bilateral airspace (alveolar) opacities involving the mid and lower lung zones bilaterally, densest in the dependent (basal) regions with a clear apical-to-basal gradient and relative apical sparing; air bronchogram-like lucencies are present in the mid zones. Both hemidiaphragms and costophrenic angles are obscured, consistent with associated pleural effusion and/or basilar consolidation/atelectasis. The cardiomediastinal silhouette appears enlarged, though its borders are obscured by the adjacent opacities and AP magnification limits true size assessment. An enteric (NG/OG) tube descends the midline (tip not clearly visualized in the hazy lower field); ECG monitoring leads/electrodes over both upper hemithoraces and additional external lines are present, including a coiled catheter/looped tube in the left mid-chest. No pneumothorax and no focal mass or nodule are identified.
impression: Diffuse bilateral airspace opacification with a dependent (basal) distribution and obscured costophrenic angles, most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic) with probable bilateral pleural effusions; bilateral/multifocal pneumonia is the main alternative. Clinical correlation recommended.
limitations: Single portable AP (likely supine/semi-upright) frontal view; no lateral view and no prior comparison. AP projection magnifies the cardiomediastinal silhouette and the cardiac borders are obscured by adjacent opacities (silhouette sign), so cardiac size is indeterminate. Supine/dependent positioning makes effusions layer posteriorly as diffuse basal haziness, so effusion cannot be reliably separated from basilar consolidation/atelectasis. The lower thorax is hazy and low-contrast, and the enteric tube tip could not be localized. Superimposed external devices (ECG leads, lines) produce artifacts. Model caveats: PSPNet lung segmentation failed on this severely opacified film (masks spanned the whole frame) and was not used for box geometry; the DenseNet 'mass' score (0.63) was discounted as unsupported visually and contradicted by ResNet (0.08). Pretrained-model scores are adjunctive, not a substitute for visual assessment.

findings: Portable supine AP chest radiograph (on-film AP marker, L badge, low contrast). Bilateral basilar opacities: the left lower zone shows a confluent hazy opacity with blunting of the left costophrenic angle and obscuration of the left hemidiaphragm and left heart border (silhouette sign), consistent with a left pleural effusion with adjacent atelectasis/consolidation; the right mid-lower zone shows a mottled, patchy, heterogeneous opacity, consistent with a right lower lobe infiltrate/consolidation +/- atelectasis. A right-sided central venous catheter is present, coursing from the right subclavian region along the mediastinum with its tip in the lower SVC/right atrial junction region (appropriate position). Multiple external ECG monitoring leads overlie the chest. The upper and mid lung zones are relatively clear. No pneumothorax. No discrete pulmonary nodule or mass. The cardiac silhouette is not clearly enlarged (manual CTR approximately 0.44-0.50, indeterminate on AP with the left border obscured).
impression: Bilateral basilar opacities on a portable supine AP film, most consistent with a left pleural effusion with adjacent atelectasis and a right lower lobe infiltrate/consolidation; early pulmonary edema cannot be excluded. Right-sided central venous catheter in appropriate position. No pneumothorax.
limitations: Single portable supine AP view (no PA/lateral correlation); low image contrast and quality; overlying external ECG leads and on-film markers (L badge, arrow, AP) limit assessment; supine position layers pleural fluid posteriorly, so effusions appear as diffuse basilar haze rather than a meniscus; the left heart border is obscured by the left base opacity (silhouette sign), making the cardiothoracic ratio unreliable; no prior films for comparison. Model-based outputs were used only as cross-checks: the view classifier gave a spurious Lateral prediction and the PSPNet segmentation was unreliable on this film (both discarded); classifier/CLIP scores cannot distinguish effusion from consolidation on a single view. Findings were verified visually in the original image before reporting.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A hazy, ill-defined airspace opacity is present in the left mid and lower lung zones, partially obscuring the left heart border and the left hemidiaphragm; the left lung field is less lucent than the right (the left basal region is measurably denser than the mirrored right basal region). An indwelling catheter is present in the left mid hemithorax with a looped course and a small dense metallic focus at its tip (a device, not a lesion). A small (~5 mm) elongated focus in the left mid lung is indeterminate (vessel in oblique section vs tiny nodule). Both lung apices are clear with no pneumothorax. The cardiac silhouette is not clearly enlarged. No definite pleural effusion or meniscus at either costophrenic angle, although both are partly obscured by large bilateral breast shadows.
impression: Left mid and lower zone hazy airspace opacity, most consistent with an infiltrate/consolidation (pneumonia) or atelectasis; a small associated effusion cannot be excluded. Indwelling left-sided catheter in situ. No pneumothorax or cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single frontal view with no prior for comparison. Large bilateral breast shadows obscure the lower lung zones and both costophrenic angles, limiting assessment of small effusions. The L/R orientation marker is ambiguous. PSPNet diaphragm and heart masks were unreliable on this image, so diaphragm height and the cardiothoracic ratio are only approximate. Pretrained model scores are not calibrated on this image (breast shadows and the catheter are off-distribution); a wrist-trauma YOLO model and a community bone-fracture classifier were run and rejected as out-of-domain. The small left-mid focus cannot be distinguished from a vessel in oblique section without a lateral view or CT.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph. A hazy, patchy, reticular opacity occupies the right lower zone (right lung base), overlying a markedly elevated right hemidiaphragm (right lung base measured ~238 px higher than the left); the opacity has an ill-defined, feathery superior border and no crisp concave meniscus. The right internal cardiac border is obscured by this basal opacity. A right internal jugular central venous catheter is present, with its tip projected over the superior vena cava / upper right atrium (precise tip position limited by the single oblique AP view). Multiple external ECG electrodes overlie the chest wall, and a dense external electrode/snap is seen over the left shoulder. The left lung is comparatively clear; the gastric bubble is visible under the left hemidiaphragm. No pneumothorax is identified (lung markings reach the periphery), no discrete focal nodule or mass is seen, and no definite rib fracture is identified. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent, but size cannot be reliably assessed on this AP view.
impression: Right lower zone opacity overlying a markedly elevated right hemidiaphragm, most consistent with right lower lobe atelectasis, with a possible small accompanying right pleural effusion. Right internal jugular central venous catheter in situ. No pneumothorax.
limitations: Single AP portable projection: cardiac size and mediastinal detail are unreliable (AP magnification, possible rotation, and the right heart border is obscured by the basal opacity), so cardiomegaly is indeterminate. No lateral view to separate anterior vs posterior basal pathology or to delineate a small effusion. External devices (ECG electrodes, central line) overlie the lung fields and can mimic or obscure findings (and inflated the DenseNet 'Mass' score, which was rejected as a false positive). Pretrained models (PSPNet, DenseNet, BiomedCLIP) were used only as supporting evidence; PSPNet under-segmented the heart (CT ratio discarded) and over-segmented the diaphragm class, and DenseNet outputs were downsampled to 224 px. 8-bit image with some low-contrast banding. The atelectasis-vs-effusion-vs-infiltrate distinction for the right basal opacity remains uncertain.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (single view, L marker present). Hazy, patchy-streaky opacity in the medial right lower zone, abutting the right heart border and right hemidiaphragm (right base intensity ~10-15 units above the mirrored left base in the parenchymal zone). Both costophrenic angles are sharp; no pleural effusion or pneumothorax seen. Cardiac silhouette of normal size (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.37-0.39). Trachea midline. Lung fields otherwise clear. Fine hair-like low-density streaks over the left cervical/paraspinal soft tissues, consistent with external artifact.
impression: Right lower zone patchy opacity, most consistent with basal atelectasis or early/mild consolidation (pneumonia). No other acute cardiopulmonary finding.
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral), so subtle posterior effusion or retrocardiac pathology cannot be excluded; PA vs AP not determined (affects CT-ratio thresholds). Pretrained classifiers disagree on this subtle finding (DenseNet flags lung opacity; ResNet essentially negative) and were not relied upon for the finding itself. MedSAM could not outline the opacity boundary. Out-of-domain wrist/fracture models were rejected (one produced a spurious 'Fractured' result). PSPNet diaphragm mask over-segmented, making the CT ratio a lower bound. Right heart border partially obscured by the opacity.

findings: Markedly elevated left hemidiaphragm (~56 px above the right, reversed from normal) with a large gastric air bubble below it (gastric distension) showing a flat air-fluid level. Left lower lobe atelectasis/volume loss secondary to the elevated diaphragm. Right upper chest: circular catheter/port device with a catheter coursing inferomedially toward the mediastinum. Right mid lung: small ring-shaped hyperdense object. Left upper chest over the clavicle and upper ribs: multiple discrete hyperdense oval metallic fragments/clips. Right lung is well aerated. No pleural effusion, no pneumothorax, no focal mass. Cardiomediastinal silhouette not widened; left heart border partly obscured by the elevated diaphragm and gastric bubble.
impression: Markedly elevated left hemidiaphragm due to a large gastric bubble (gastric distension) with secondary left basilar atelectasis. Incidental right-sided catheter/port device, a small ring device, and left upper chest metallic clips/fragments. No acute cardiopulmonary process.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral/oblique), so depth and subdiaphragmatic localization are limited; patient position (upright vs supine) is uncertain, which affects the air-fluid-level interpretation. The left heart border and left lung base are obscured by the elevated diaphragm and gastric bubble, limiting assessment of cardiomegaly and left lower lobe disease. The image is an 8-bit rescaled radiograph and the device-like objects are only intermediate density, limiting certainty about their composition. Pretrained pathology classifiers (DenseNet, ResNet) were non-specific and mutually inconsistent on this atypical image and were not used to support any finding. Bounding boxes are in original 1024x1024 pixel coordinates [x, y, w, h].

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (L marker present). Both lungs are well expanded and well aerated with normal pulmonary vascular markings; no focal consolidation, mass, nodule or infiltrate is identified in either lung. The right and left costophrenic angles are both sharp, with no pleural effusion and no pneumothorax. The cardiac silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.48) with sharp borders; the mediastinum is of normal width and the trachea is midline. Both hemidiaphragms are at normal levels with the right dome slightly higher (normal), and a normal gastric air bubble is seen below the left dome. No rib fracture, lytic lesion or other osseous abnormality is identified. An external L marker and a lead are seen over the left shoulder. The initial visual impression of a left lower zone opacity was refuted by pixel-level, enhancement and segmentation analyses: that density corresponds to the normal left heart border, hemidiaphragm and gastric region.
impression: Normal chest radiograph. No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality and no focal lesion identified.
limitations: Single frontal view without a lateral or decubitus projection, so subtle retrocardiac, apical or posterior processes cannot be fully excluded. The projection (PA vs AP) is not labeled and the scapulae partially overlap the lung fields, which limits precise assessment of cardiac size. An external marker/lead over the left shoulder may obscure a small area. Pretrained model outputs were partially uninformative: the ResNet-50 (512) classifier was negative for all pathologies, while several DenseNet-121 (224) variants gave mild non-specific chronic-label scores and the CheXpert-trained variant gave mild edema/cardiomegaly/fracture signals without any visual correlate; a zero-shot vision-language probe failed a sanity check on a normal lung crop and was recorded as untrusted; the PSPNet segmentation under-segmented the heart. Residual uncertainty about very subtle parenchymal disease therefore remains.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (AP-type projection, L marker; supine/monitored patient). Multiple ECG electrodes and leads overlie the chest. A right-sided percutaneous catheter enters near the right apex/axilla with its coiled (pigtail) metallic tip within a focal rounded opacity in the right mid-zone (approx 8 cm, x156-309/y488-662), with a cluster of air lucencies adjacent to the tip. A second tube enters at the right lateral chest wall with its tip in the medial right base (approx x160,y690 to x450,y698). Streaky band-like opacity (plate-like/subsegmental atelectasis) in the right lower zone (x196-424/y669-786) with mottled aeration. Cardiac silhouette at the upper limit of normal (cardiothoracic ratio approx 0.50 on this magnifying AP film); no definite cardiomegaly. Trachea midline; mediastinum not widened. Left lung clear, left costophrenic angle sharp, normal gastric bubble. No definite pneumothorax (apical and mid-zone lung markings reach the chest wall; no pleural line on enhanced inspection), no large pleural effusion or air-fluid level, no rib fracture. A tiny faint curvilinear density near the left heart border (approx x705,y560) is of indeterminate significance.
impression: Focal rounded right mid-zone opacity with internal air and a pigtail catheter tip in situ, plus right basilar atelectasis, in a patient with right-sided drainage tubes: most consistent with a right mid-zone consolidation/collapse process (e.g., pneumonia/abscess or post-obstructive atelectasis) under active percutaneous drainage; loculated right pleural collection (empyema) and right lung mass remain in the differential. No pneumothorax or large effusion.
limitations: Single frontal (AP-type, likely supine) view only; no lateral view and no prior films for comparison. AP projection magnifies the cardiac silhouette, making the CTR of ~0.50 borderline and cardiomegaly indeterminate. Multiple overlying ECG electrodes, leads and two right-sided tubes partially obscure the right hemithorax and complicate tracing of the catheters. The character of the mid-zone opacity (consolidation vs collapse vs mass vs loculated collection) cannot be definitively resolved without contrast imaging or further views. A small/loculated right pleural effusion and a tiny indeterminate density near the left heart border cannot be excluded. Pretrained segmentation models (PSPNet, UNetResNet50) failed to delineate the heart and collapsed right lung on this image and were discarded for measurement; out-of-domain detectors (wrist-trauma YOLO, community bone-fracture classifier) were run only as negative controls and their outputs were not used.

findings: AP portable frontal chest radiograph with an L marker; skeletal appearance is consistent with a pediatric or adolescent patient (age not verifiable from the image). The cardiac silhouette is prominent, with a segmented cardiothoracic ratio of approximately 0.61, exceeding the adult 0.50 cutoff but magnified by the AP projection. There is a faint, ill-defined area of increased opacity in the left lower lung zone, most marked in the medial (retrocardiac) and mid regions above the left hemidiaphragm; a mirror-asymmetry analysis shows the left lower zone is denser than the contralateral region (mean intensity difference +27 in the medial zone, +7 laterally) and a prompted segmentation delineates a coherent region of altered density above the diaphragm. The left lateral costophrenic angle is sharp, arguing against a significant pleural effusion. The right lung base is well aerated with a sharp costophrenic angle; no focal right-sided opacity was confirmed. The trachea is midline.
