impression: Mild left lower zone airspace opacity (retrocardiac hazy density, sharp costophrenic angle), most consistent with atelectasis or early consolidation, together with borderline mild cardiomegaly on an AP portable film (segmented CTR approx 0.61, with AP magnification). No pneumothorax or significant pleural effusion.
limitations: Single AP portable frontal view without PA or lateral comparison, so retrocardiac opacity cannot be separated from effusion by additional projections and AP magnification inflates the cardiothoracic ratio. Patient age is not stated on the image; the skeletal appearance suggests a pediatric or adolescent patient, which shifts the normal CTR threshold. The left lower zone opacity is subtle and partly obscured by the heart and diaphragm. Pretrained classifier scores are in conflict on cardiomegaly (one model positive, one negative) and were used only as supporting evidence; the 14-structure PSPNet model failed to produce usable masks on this film and was discarded. No dedicated rib series was performed.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. The cardiac silhouette is enlarged, with a measured transverse cardiac-to-thoracic ratio of approximately 0.65-0.69 at the diaphragm level (AP projection overestimates size). Bilateral mid-to-lower zone interstitial and patchy parenchymal opacities: coarse reticular pattern with perihilar accentuation and peribronchial thickening, worst basally, without definite confluent consolidation or air bronchograms. No definite pleural effusion and no pneumothorax; costophrenic angles not clearly blunted. Multiple small, discrete, bone-density foci (one ring/ovoid with lucent center, several short straight rod-like) clustered in the left axillary soft tissues, lateral to the chest wall - calcified axillary lymph nodes, with surgical clips as a differential. A thin, smooth, uniform, two-walled linear structure runs over the right lower lateral chest wall and onto the abdomen, outside the thoracic cavity, consistent with an external object (drain/tubing/lead). Both humeral heads show a mottled, coarse trabecular pattern (bilateral and roughly symmetric), most consistent with degenerative/osteopenic change.
impression: Cardiomegaly with bilateral mid-to-lower zone interstitial/parenchymal opacities, most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic) with possible superimposed atelectasis or early pneumonia, on a portable AP film. Additionally: calcified axillary foci (vs surgical clips) in the left axilla, an external linear object (drain/tube/lead) over the right lower lateral chest wall, and bilateral mottled humeral heads (degenerative/osteopenic).
limitations: Single portable AP view: cardiac width is overestimated by magnification and no lateral view is available to confirm depth/localization; 8-bit PNG with compressed dynamic range prevents reliable metallic-vs-calcific HU assessment and absolute density quantification; no prior studies for comparison; shoulder girdle superimposes the lung apices; model-based caveats: PSPNet anatomy segmentation failed validation on this AP film and its CTR was discarded (manual verified borders used instead), calibrated op_norm classifier outputs were non-discriminative, and BiomedCLIP is zero-shot/uncalibrated (used as corroboration only); the bilateral mottled humeral heads and the external linear object over the right lower chest/abdominal wall are reported as observations but not boxed as focal lesions; no clinical context available.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A small (~4-6 mm), well-circumscribed, round opacity (nodule) is present in the left mid lung zone, intraparenchymal and between the ribs, not contiguous with an identifiable vessel. The right hilum appears mildly prominent and soft without a discrete round mass, consistent with normal hilar vascular confluence (mild right hilar fullness). Several other 2-4 mm round opacities in both lungs are arranged along vascular paths and are most consistent with pulmonary vessels in cross-section. No focal consolidation, pleural effusion, pneumothorax or atelectasis. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.47) and contour, trachea midline. Both costophrenic angles are sharp. Osseous structures appear intact on this projection.
impression: Small left mid-zone pulmonary nodule (differential includes pulmonary vessel in cross-section); no other acute cardiopulmonary abnormality. Comparison with prior imaging or short-interval follow-up is recommended to confirm stability of the nodule.
limitations: Single frontal projection; no lateral view and no prior imaging for comparison. The film is overpenetrated with low lung-to-mediastinum contrast (~20 gray levels), limiting assessment of subtle hilar/mediastinal detail and of very small lesions. Physical pixel spacing is unknown, so lesion size is estimated in pixels (~0.35 mm/px). Nodule versus vessel-in-cross-section cannot be definitively distinguished on a single frontal film. Pretrained classifiers were near their operating thresholds (DenseNet121: Mass 0.55, Nodule 0.52, Lung Opacity 0.55; ResNet50: Nodule 0.19, Mass 0.06) and were used only as supporting, not primary, evidence; two ResNet50 labels (Lung Lesion, Enlarged Cardiomediastinum) have NaN operating thresholds and their 0.5 outputs are defaults, not predictions. The YOLOv8 wrist-trauma detector was out of domain (it flagged burned-in text and a spurious 'fracture' on shoulder soft tissue) and was rejected. A burned-in 'L' marker and a blacked-out header occupy the top-right corner.

findings: Frontal (AP, likely portable) chest radiograph of a monitored/intubated patient. Support devices: endotracheal tube with tip above the carina, enteric tube with distal end in the left upper abdomen, a coiled right-sided central venous catheter projecting over the right upper lung with its tip over the right mid lung (likely a pulmonary artery catheter or kinked CVC; device, not a lesion), and external ECG leads. Diffuse bilateral air-space opacification with air bronchograms in the right mid lung, most prominent in the right mid and both lower zones (right greater than left). Dense bilateral basal white-out with flat/slightly concave upper borders obscuring both hemidiaphragms and both costophrenic angles, consistent with moderate bilateral pleural effusions with underlying collapse/consolidation. Widened cardiomediastinal silhouette; cardiac size not reliably assessable because of the adjacent opacity and AP magnification. No pneumothorax. No definite rib fracture.
impression: Diffuse bilateral air-space disease with right-predominant consolidation (air bronchograms) and moderate bilateral pleural effusions in an intubated patient; most consistent with bilateral pneumonia with parapneumonic effusions, with cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema remaining in the differential. The coiled right-sided central catheter (tip over the right mid lung) warrants position review.
limitations: Single frontal (AP, likely portable/supine) view: effusion versus consolidation/atelectasis cannot be separated in the bases; cardiac size cannot be reliably assessed (obscured borders, AP magnification); no lateral or decubitus views; washed-out underpenetrated image and bottom letterbox bar reduce contrast and confound automated tools; pixel values are not physically calibrated after rescaling; a coiled catheter projects over the right upper lung (device, not a lesion); pretrained model outputs were only trustworthy after correcting input normalization for the 8-bit source (maxval=255); PSPNet anatomical masks and MedSAM segmentations were partially unreliable on this image and were not used for final box boundaries.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph, adequately penetrated and inspired. Both lungs are well expanded and essentially clear; no focal consolidation, mass, pleural effusion or pneumothorax. Cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size and contour, trachea midline, hila not enlarged. Costophrenic angles are sharp bilaterally. A small (~4-5 mm) round, slightly ill-defined soft-tissue opacity is present in the left mid-lung zone (lateral) - a small pulmonary nodule. A second, fainter small round calcified-appearing opacity lies over the left heart border (possible tiny calcified granuloma or lymph node). Multiple surgical clips are seen in the right axilla / right lateral chest wall, consistent with prior surgery. The right upper zone is slightly more lucent than the left, most consistent with projectional asymmetry (no discrete bulla wall or pleural line). No acute osseous abnormality identified.
impression: Small (~4 mm) indeterminate pulmonary nodule in the left mid-lung zone, with a faint tiny calcified opacity over the left heart border and incidental right-axillary surgical clips; no acute cardiopulmonary process. Correlate with prior imaging; if none available, consider short-interval follow-up CT to characterize the nodule.
limitations: Single frontal projection only: no lateral/oblique view and no prior comparison, so the nodule cannot be separated from a vessel-on-end or assigned to a lobe/segment. 8-bit PNG display windowing may hide very low-contrast detail. The nodule is small (~4 mm) and near the detection limit: both deep-learning classifiers run on this image did not flag a nodule (consistent with its sub-pixel size after 224/512 downsampling), so their negative nodule scores were not used to discount the directly seen opacity. The right upper-zone lucent asymmetry is probably projectional and was not characterized further. Pretrained model outputs were used as cross-checks, not as sole support for any finding.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A subtle, ill-defined mild opacity is present in the right mid lung zone, abutting the right heart border, without a definite silhouette sign or air bronchograms; it is the only soft-tissue abnormality. The lungs are otherwise well aerated with no discrete mass, nodule, or lobar consolidation. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approx. 0.46) and the trachea is midline. No pleural effusion (sharp costophrenic angles) and no pneumothorax. An external metallic clip-like object, consistent with an ECG lead/electrode, overlies the left shoulder soft tissues; the underlying clavicle, scapula and humerus are intact (external artifact, not a thoracic lesion).
impression: Subtle mild right mid-zone pulmonary opacity, most consistent with an early/mild infiltrate (or mild atelectasis), on an otherwise unremarkable frontal chest radiograph; no acute cardiopulmonary process. External ECG-type artifact over the left shoulder.
limitations: Single frontal projection (no lateral view), limiting depth localization. The right mid-zone opacity is subtle and ill-defined and could partly reflect a normal asymmetric pulmonary vascular pattern or projection; no lateral view or follow-up is available to confirm. Portable/AP acquisition can alter the apparent cardiac silhouette and fluid distribution. An external metallic artifact over the left shoulder obscures the left shoulder/upper zone. Pretrained pathology-classifier scores were borderline (near the operating threshold) and were used only as supporting hypotheses, not as the basis for the finding. Interpretation is from a single static image without clinical history.

findings: Frontal (likely AP) chest radiograph of a female patient with bilateral breast shadows and an external beaded chain/necklace overlying the neck and upper thoracic spine. The cardiac silhouette is enlarged and globular (cardiomegaly), with the left heart border bulging laterally; the measured cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.50. The aortic knob appears prominent (smooth left upper mediastinal contour). There is a mild, non-specific increased density at the right lung base that may represent mild atelectasis or overlapping diaphragm/breast shadow; no definite consolidation. The remaining lung fields are clear. No pneumothorax. The right costophrenic angle is sharp; the left is partially obscured by the breast shadow, with no definite pleural effusion. Hila are not markedly enlarged. No acute osseous abnormality.
impression: Cardiomegaly (enlarged globular cardiac silhouette) on a frontal, likely AP, chest radiograph. No definite acute pulmonary process (no consolidation, effusion, or pneumothorax). Prominent aortic knob and mild right base density are non-specific.
limitations: Single frontal (likely AP) projection: AP geometry magnifies the cardiac silhouette and overestimates the cardiothoracic ratio (measured ~0.50, at the cardiomegaly threshold), so true cardiac size may be smaller. Bilateral breast shadows obscure the lower lung zones and part of the left hemidiaphragm/costophrenic angle. An external chain/necklace overlies the neck/upper thoracic spine and could mimic calcification or a device. The mild right base density is non-specific and confounded by overlying diaphragm and breast tissue. No lateral view or prior films for comparison. Pretrained classifier outputs are image-level (no localization) and were used only as corroborating evidence; the out-of-domain wrist detector was rejected as untrustworthy.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. A large, dense, well-circumscribed, rounded and lobulated opacity occupies the left upper and mid zone, with a small residual aerated crescent at the left apex, an elevated left hilum and an elevated left hemidiaphragm, a pattern consistent with a mass and associated left upper lobe volume loss/collapse. A separate discrete rounded opacity (nodule) is seen in the right lower lung, just above the right hemidiaphragm. Hazy increased density is present at the left base with partial obscuration of the left costophrenic angle, and a gastric air-fluid level lies below the elevated left hemidiaphragm (indeterminate atelectasis or small effusion). Orthopedic hardware (multiple screws) is present over the right clavicle and shoulder, and a central venous catheter is in situ with its tip projecting over the SVC/cavoatrial region. No pneumothorax is identified. The left heart border is obscured by the left upper mass, so cardiomegaly cannot be assessed.
impression: Large left upper zone mass with associated left upper lobe collapse, plus a right basal pulmonary nodule; the findings are concerning for a primary lung malignancy with a possible contralateral lesion, although infection and other causes are not excluded on this single view.
limitations: Single frontal projection without a lateral view, so depth and exact anatomical attribution are limited. Portable-quality image with slight rotation and soft-tissue bulk, reducing detail in the lower zones. The left upper mass obscures the left heart border, so cardiomegaly cannot be assessed. The right basal opacity is indeterminate in character (nodule vs mass vs rounded atelectasis). Left basal haziness is indeterminate (atelectasis vs small effusion). Pretrained classifiers and segmentation models were trained mainly on hospital PA films, and portable films may affect their reliability; the MedSAM and PSPNet delineations are approximate and were verified visually. No clinical history is available and none is inferred from the image.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (L marker present; PA vs AP not confirmed). Cardiac silhouette within normal limits: cardiothoracic ratio measured at 0.41-0.47 across levels (max 0.465, below the 0.50 criterion; borderline upper-normal). Lungs are well expanded with normal branching vascular markings; no focal consolidation, mass, nodule, pneumothorax, or pulmonary edema. Hila unremarkable. Both costophrenic angles are preserved at 4x magnification; no pleural effusion. Mild non-specific haziness in the right lower zone, most consistent with breast shadow overlap and dense normal vasculature; no definite focal atelectasis or airspace opacity. Trachea midline, mediastinum not widened. No acute osseous abnormality. A bright curved radiopaque object in the right lower quadrant (x~30-420, y~880-1020) lies outside the body contour and is an external monitoring device, not a finding.
impression: No acute cardiopulmonary abnormality and no focal lesion identified on this single frontal view; borderline-normal cardiac silhouette (CTR ~0.46). Weak classifier signals (cardiomegaly, effusion, lung opacity) were not corroborated on direct inspection or by quantitative measurement and are not reported as findings.
limitations: Single frontal view; AP vs PA projection unconfirmed (AP projection exaggerates cardiac size, so the CTR-based 'no cardiomegaly' conclusion is conservative). Central overpenetration and 8-bit PNG quantization limit detection of subtle opacities and make cardiac borders imprecise (+/-10-15 px); breast shadows obscure the lower zones and the left costophrenic angle. Pretrained classifiers disagree: DenseNet121 (all and NIH weights) scored cardiomegaly/effusion/opacity/lung-opacity above their calibrated thresholds but these were contradicted by the measured CTR, by the negative ResNet50 and zero-shot BiomedCLIP outputs, and by direct inspection at 2x-4x, so they were not relied upon; the PSPNet heart mask under-segments and fragments the cardiac silhouette. No lateral view available.

findings: Frontal (PA) chest radiograph. Right mid-zone: focal dense round-oval opacity adjacent to the right hilum, approximately 3 cm, with somewhat irregular lobulated margins and fine spiculation superiorly; the horizontal (minor) fissure below it is thickened. Right lower zone: reticulonodular patchy consolidation extending from the mid-zone to the base, with a dense homogeneous opacity at the right base whose upper border is smooth and dome-shaped, consistent with an elevated right hemidiaphragm (subpulmonic effusion not excludable). The right heart border and right hemidiaphragm are obscured. Left mid-zone: small (~1 cm) faint round opacity overlapping a posterior rib, indeterminate between a pulmonary nodule and an osseous/superimposed structure. Trachea midline; left lung otherwise clear with sharp left costophrenic angle; no pneumothorax; no definite rib fracture; no definite cardiomegaly.
impression: Right mid-zone/perihilar lung mass with associated right lower lobe reticulonodular consolidation and dense right basal opacity with elevated right hemidiaphragm, findings most suggestive of bronchogenic malignancy with post-obstructive change; a small indeterminate left mid-zone opacity overlies a posterior rib.
limitations: Single frontal projection only (no lateral view) and no prior images for comparison. The right heart border, right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are obscured by the overlying opacity; subpulmonic effusion vs true diaphragmatic elevation at the right base cannot be distinguished. The small left opacity overlies a posterior rib, so its pulmonary vs osseous nature is indeterminate. The right upper zone is partly obscured by the right scapula. AI model outputs are supportive but not diagnostic: single-dataset MIMIC/CheXpert DenseNet variants and zero-shot BiomedCLIP scores were judged unreliable on this image and were not relied upon; MedSAM and PSPNet masks were used only for extent/anatomical reference.

findings: Frontal (likely portable AP) chest radiograph of a post-sternotomy patient (midline sternal wires), with a right shoulder ORIF plate, multiple small metallic surgical clips/anchors (right shoulder, left axilla, overlying the heart), and overlying external monitoring cables. Bilateral basal opacities, right markedly greater than left: a large dense homogeneous right lower-zone opacity that obscures the right hemidiaphragm and the right heart border (upper border at approximately y=445) with a blunted right costophrenic angle, and a smaller left lower-zone opacity that blunts the left costophrenic angle and obscures the left hemidiaphragm (upper border at approximately y=585). Low lung volumes. Upper lung zones are aerated with no focal mass or nodule. No pneumothorax (both apices aerated, no pleural line). The lower cardiomediastinal silhouette is obscured and its size cannot be measured.
impression: Bilateral basal opacities (right > left) in a post-cardiac-surgery patient, most consistent with pleural effusion and/or post-operative atelectasis. No pneumothorax and no focal mass. Cardiomegaly cannot be excluded because the cardiac silhouette is obscured.
limitations: Single frontal (likely supine/portable AP) view; no lateral view, so the anterior-posterior extent of the opacities cannot be determined. The cardiomediastinal silhouette and both hemidiaphragms are obscured by the basal opacities, so cardiac size and effusion volume cannot be measured. Extensive metallic hardware (sternal wires, shoulder plate, surgical clips) and overlying external monitoring cables limit assessment and can cause false-positive classifier responses (e.g. 'mass', 'fracture'). Effusion, atelectasis and consolidation cannot be fully distinguished on a single supine film. The pretrained classifiers were trained on frontal chest radiographs without this degree of surgical hardware, so their scores are corroborative rather than definitive.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (PA/AP) showing two focal intrapulmonary opacities. (1) A well-circumscribed, round, homogeneous opacity of approximately 4 cm in the right mid lung zone (right middle lobe region), with slightly lobulated margins. (2) A smaller, rounded opacity of approximately 3 cm in the left mid lung zone with somewhat less sharp margins. The left hilum shows a normal vascular confluence without a discrete mass. The cardiac silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.34). Both costophrenic angles are sharp with no pleural effusion. No pneumothorax. The trachea is midline. No rib or clavicular fracture is visible. No other focal opacities are identified in the lung fields.
impression: Two focal pulmonary opacities: a round mass in the right mid lung zone and a smaller nodule in the left mid lung zone. The bilateral rounded opacities in different lobes are most consistent with metastatic pulmonary disease or a primary lung malignancy with a contralateral metastasis. No other acute cardiopulmonary finding.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view and no prior for comparison). The image was resampled to a 1024x1024 square, so aspect-ratio distortion is possible and cm sizes (assuming ~25 cm thoracic width) are approximate. A rotated corner label ('L 020') and dark corner vignette are present and confounded the whole-image pathology classifiers, which emitted spurious 'Fracture'/'Enlarged Cardiomediastinum' signals and scored the visible Mass/Nodule as absent; those classifier outputs were judged unreliable and were not used to support any finding. Localization relied on visually verified UNetResNet50 anatomical segmentation and MedSAM prompted segmentation, which are approximate at lesion margins. No CT is available, so internal mass characteristics (necrosis, calcification, spiculation) cannot be fully characterized.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (L marker present). A large, well-circumscribed, rounded, homogeneous soft-tissue-density opacity occupies the right lower hemithorax/right upper quadrant (approx x90-445, y515-840); its top border coincides with the right hemidiaphragm on two independent segmentation models, the right hemidiaphragm is mildly elevated, and a cluster of 3-4 small surgical clips lies within it. No meniscus, no rising lateral edge and no mediastinal (tracheal) shift, arguing against a free-flowing pleural effusion. A right chest-wall port is present with its catheter looping in the right upper zone and descending toward the right lower mediastinum (tip not clearly visualized); a second thin line/catheter runs from the right axilla through the right subclavian vein with its tip in the infraclavicular region (not in the SVC). Two crossing surgical clips are seen in the right upper mediastinum (right paratracheal). No pneumothorax. No significant right lung parenchymal opacity (right mid-zone intensity 108.0 vs mirrored left 107.6; the apparent haziness on CLAHE is an enhancement artifact). Cardiac silhouette top-normal (classifier cardiomegaly scores <=0.14). Left lung clear; bowel gas below both hemidiaphragms. The apparent thin lucent rim around the basal opacity is not true gas (no pixels <45 in the region).
impression: Dominant finding: a large well-circumscribed rounded subdiaphragmatic (hepatic-region) opacity in the right upper quadrant with embedded surgical clips and mild right hemidiaphragm elevation, most consistent with a hepatic mass or subdiaphragmatic collection in a post-surgical patient (prominent/enlarged liver is the main alternative). Two lines/devices: a right chest port with catheter, and a second right axillary-subclavian catheter whose tip has not reached the SVC. No acute cardiopulmonary process: no effusion, no pneumothorax, no focal lung opacity, no cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single frontal 8-bit projection without a lateral view, so depth localization is limited and the subdiaphragmatic (vs basal pleural) location of the rounded opacity relies on two independent segmentation models plus 2D border/shift analysis, which agree. The 8-bit export compresses dynamic range; the character of the rounded opacity (mass vs collection vs prominent liver) cannot be established without additional views or CT, and the surgical history it suggests is unknown. The port catheter tip and the axillary-subclavian line tip could not be definitively traced due to overlap with the dense basal opacity and bone. Model outputs were used only after sanity checks: BiomedCLIP gave flat uniform zero-shot scores (rejected) and the out-of-domain wrist models (YOLO GRAZPEDWRI, community fracture classifier) gave meaningless outputs (rejected); a CLAHE-suggested right mid-zone opacity was refuted by quantitative right-vs-left comparison (108.0 vs 107.6) and excluded. No clinical history available.

findings: AP portable chest radiograph. A focal, hazy, heterogeneous airspace opacity occupies the right mid and lower zone, extending from the right lateral chest wall medially to the heart border and from a curvilinear superior margin (consistent with an elevated fissure or lobar border) down to the right hemidiaphragm; bronchovascular markings are seen through it and no meniscus or air-fluid level is identified. The cardiac silhouette is borderline enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio ~0.50, magnified by the AP projection) with a globular contour and prominent left heart border. The left costophrenic angle is partially obscured by basal haziness without a definite meniscus. Devices: an endotracheal/tracheostomy tube in the trachea and a central venous (likely dialysis) catheter with two parallel lumens and a coiled tip in the right mid hemithorax. No pneumothorax, no rib fracture, no definite pleural effusion. A horizontal beam/bed artifact crosses the inferior edge.
impression: Right mid/lower zone pulmonary infiltrate (pneumonia/consolidation most likely, atelectasis in the differential) in a critically ill patient with endotracheal intubation and a central venous catheter; borderline cardiac silhouette, likely magnified by the portable AP projection. No pneumothorax or definite pleural effusion.
limitations: Single portable AP view (no PA or lateral): cardiac and mediastinal magnification and rotation limit the cardiothoracic ratio, which is borderline (~0.50); supine/semi-erect positioning can mask or shift small effusions; the film is hazy and somewhat under-penetrated, blunting costophrenic angle assessment; indwelling catheters and the airway tube overlie the right hemithorax and can mimic or obscure pathology; left basal haziness could not be separated into a definite focal lesion; pretrained models were trained predominantly on PA films, so their (negative) cardiomegaly and effusion scores are discounted on this projection; zero-shot and out-of-domain model outputs were used only as sanity checks, not as evidence.

findings: Upright frontal chest radiograph. Large right pleural effusion: a dense, homogeneous opacity fills the right lower hemithorax with a concave-up (meniscus) upper margin that rises toward the lateral chest wall (crest at approx. x=230, y=500), obliterating the right costophrenic angle and right hemidiaphragm and obscuring the right heart border. Associated right lower zone compressive atelectasis. The left lung is clear with a sharp left costophrenic angle. The trachea is midline with no significant mediastinal shift. No pneumothorax, no focal mass or nodule, and no definite rib fracture. A thin, uniform radiopaque line over the left lateral chest wall is an external monitoring line, not an indwelling device. Cardiac size is difficult to assess because the right heart border is obscured.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with associated compressive atelectasis; left lung clear.
limitations: Single frontal (PA/AP) view only; no lateral or decubitus view to fully separate pleural fluid from parenchymal consolidation/collapse or to confirm free-flowing behavior. The right hemidiaphragm and right heart border are obscured by the effusion, so the inferior and medial extent of the fluid cannot be precisely demarcated (the box therefore extends to the image edge). Cardiomediastinal size is incompletely assessable. Model inputs were derived from an 8-bit PNG (not raw DICOM), requiring bit-depth extension before the torchxrayvision normalization; classifier scores are global (not spatially localized) and were used only as supporting evidence. The left lower zone shows only minimal markings, not a definite lesion.

findings: Portable supine AP chest radiograph of an intubated/central-lined patient. Hazy, ill-defined opacity of the right mid-to-lower zone, extending from an ill-defined upper border (approx. 5th-6th intercostal space, slightly higher laterally) down to the bottom of the field, obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle and partially silhouetting the right heart border; ribs faintly visible through the opacity, no definite air bronchograms. Left lung well aerated without definite focal opacity or effusion (extreme left costophrenic angle not in field). Cardiac silhouette not clearly enlarged (estimated CTR ~0.43); trachea midline; no pneumothorax; no definite nodule or mass. Devices: right-sided central venous catheter with tip in the SVC (appropriate); endotracheal tube with tip ~3-4 cm above the carina (appropriate); gastric tube with tip in the stomach; implanted port in the left lower chest with cephalad catheter; multiple ECG leads.
impression: Hazy right mid-to-lower zone opacity on a portable supine AP film, most consistent with a moderate right pleural effusion (layering) with adjacent atelectasis; right lower lobe pneumonia/consolidation is a close differential. Support devices are in appropriate positions.
limitations: Single portable supine AP view; lower field cut off so costophrenic angles and the inferior extent of the opacity cannot be fully assessed; AP geometry magnifies the cardiac silhouette (CTR ~0.43 estimated manually from grid landmarks); no lateral view or prior comparison; heavy overlap of lines, leads and a port device; 8-bit PNG export with reduced dynamic range. Effusion vs consolidation vs atelectasis cannot be definitively separated on one supine film. Pretrained classifier scores are corroborative only (trained mainly on upright PA films; effusion scores are low because a supine layering effusion does not show the trained meniscus pattern). PSPNet segmentation masks were unreliable on this artifact-heavy film (class label convention mismatch and bleeding into chest wall/diaphragm) and were discarded for quantitative use; the autoencoder error map and both out-of-domain models (pediatric wrist YOLO, community fracture classifier) were uninformative and rejected.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph showing an enlarged, globular cardiac silhouette (cardiomegaly). The measured cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.53 (heart width 369-371 px vs thoracic width 699 px), corroborated by two independent segmentation models and two pathology classifiers. The lungs are clear without definite focal consolidation, mass, nodule, or pneumothorax. Costophrenic angles are preserved bilaterally with no definite pleural effusion or meniscus. The trachea is midline, mediastinal contours are unremarkable, and no rib, clavicle, or scapular fracture is identified.
impression: Cardiomegaly (enlarged cardiac silhouette) as the sole significant finding; lungs otherwise clear.
limitations: Single frontal view: PA vs AP projection cannot be determined, and AP/supine projection exaggerates heart size, so a CTR of 0.53 may overstate the degree of enlargement. No lateral view to assess retrocardiac disease or the posterior costophrenic angles. 8-bit grayscale with mild noise; the left hemidiaphragm is partly obscured by the heart, limiting evaluation of a small left effusion or retrocardiac atelectasis. Pretrained classifier outputs are probability-like scores, not locations; DenseNet showed label over-firing and was down-weighted. Out-of-domain bone models misfired and were rejected.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph of an intubated, monitored patient. Endotracheal tube with tip in the mid-trachea (appropriate position); a second tube from the right neck (likely central venous or enteric) whose tip is not confidently identified; ECG electrodes and external cables overlying the chest. Bilateral patchy alveolar (airspace) opacities, most dense in the mid and lower lung zones (right perihilar/mid-lung and left upper-mid zone). Dense bilateral basilar opacities with blunted costophrenic angles and obscured hemidiaphragms, consistent with pleural effusion and/or basilar atelectasis/consolidation. Cardiac silhouette is widened and partially obscured by adjacent opacities; the cardiothoracic ratio is borderline (~0.51-0.54, overestimated on AP). No pneumothorax and no apical consolidation identified.
impression: Bilateral patchy airspace disease with bilateral basilar opacities (likely pleural effusions, atelectasis and/or consolidation not excluded) in a mechanically ventilated patient; the pattern is consistent with pulmonary edema or multifocal pneumonia and cannot be separated on a single portable AP film. Borderline cardiac silhouette; no definite cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single portable AP view: magnification of the heart and mediastinum and reduced penetration at the bases; no lateral view and no prior images for comparison. Free pleural fluid cannot be definitively separated from basilar atelectasis or consolidation on this view, and the etiology of the bilateral airspace opacities (edema vs pneumonia vs ARDS) cannot be established by imaging alone; model evidence is only moderate and partly conflicting (DenseNet favors pneumonia, zero-shot BiomedCLIP favors edema/infiltrates, both agree on infiltration/effusion). Classifier effusion/edema scores sit at or below the random-noise baseline (see measurements/sanity_checks_classifiers.json) and were down-weighted. Overlying ECG electrodes, cables, endotracheal tube and a right-neck line (tip not identified) obscure portions of the lung fields. PSPNet cardiac segmentation was unreliable on this image, so the cardiothoracic ratio is a visual estimate.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (PA-type projection, 'L' marker over the patient's left). Ill-defined roundish soft-tissue opacity measuring approximately 4.5-5 cm in the right mid-lower lung field, with a well-demarcated round air-density lucency at its medial border (air bronchogram, peripheral cavity, or aerated lung adjacent to the lesion). Separate round, well-demarcated soft-tissue nodule of approximately 1.2 cm in the left lower lung zone. Mild, nonspecific increased interstitial markings in the left mid-lower zones (possibly within normal limits). Bilateral breast shadows overlie the lower lung fields. Cardiac silhouette not enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio proxy 0.28); trachea midline; both costophrenic angles sharp (no pleural effusion); no pneumothorax; no fracture or destructive bony lesion identified.
impression: Right lower lobe opacity (~4.5-5 cm) with a round air lucency at its border, most consistent with an infiltrate/consolidation (pneumonia, possibly with early cavitation), with a separate 1.2 cm left lower zone nodule of indeterminate significance. Round atelectasis or a mass with peripheral necrosis/cavitation cannot be excluded on a single frontal view. Chest CT recommended for characterization and staging of both lesions.
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral for anteroposterior localization); bilateral breast shadows overlie the lower lung fields; under-penetrated mediastinum; the left nodule is low-contrast, so a small end-on vessel or nipple shadow cannot be fully excluded; the right lower opacity's nature (consolidation vs mass vs atelectasis vs abscess) is not determinable on a single projection; lesion size estimates are approximate (scale derived from thoracic width); pretrained model outputs (DenseNet/ResNet scores, BiomedCLIP zero-shot, MedSAM, PSPNet) were used only as corroboration, and their Effusion, Cardiomegaly and Enlarged Cardiomediastinum flags were not visually confirmed.

findings: Portable supine AP chest radiograph in a post-sternotomy patient (sternal closure wires in the midline; multiple ECG electrodes and leads, at least one right-sided intravascular catheter, and a tube projecting over the upper abdomen). Marked elevation of the right hemidiaphragm: a sharp, smooth, concave-upward border runs from the right lateral chest wall (about x=185, y=460) to the mediastinum (about x=470, y=455), with the dome at y~430, roughly 7 cm above the left hemidiaphragm dome (y~610); the aerated right lung ends exactly at this line, with loss of right lower lobe volume (compressed/atelectatic right lung base above it). Patchy, reticular opacity in the left lower zone (retrocardiac and basal), partially obscuring the left hemidiaphragm medially; the lateral left costophrenic angle remains relatively sharp. Hazy, mottled perihilar opacity in the right mid zone. Cardiomediastinal silhouette is prominent, but the cardiothoracic ratio is approximately 0.42 (visual estimate 0.36-0.45), not meeting the threshold for cardiomegaly on this AP film. No pneumothorax (lung markings reach the pleura at both apices and mid zones), no definite pleural effusion, no free subdiaphragmatic air (the right subdiaphragmatic region measures soft-tissue density, 127-141 on the 0-255 scale), and a round gas bubble in the right upper abdomen consistent with the hepatic flexure or duodenum.
impression: Post-sternotomy, monitored ICU patient: dominant finding is marked right hemidiaphragm elevation with right lower lobe atelectasis (volume loss); patchy left lower zone opacity most consistent with atelectasis (early infiltrate not excluded) and a hazy right perihilar opacity. No pneumothorax, no definite effusion, no free air, no definite cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single supine portable AP film: cardiac magnification and reduced sensitivity for small pneumothorax, small effusions, and small amounts of free air; no lateral or prior views for comparison. Multiple overlying devices (sternal wires, ECG leads, catheters/tubes) obscure portions of the lung fields and mediastinum. The right heart border is silhouetted by the elevated right hemidiaphragm/liver, so the cardiothoracic ratio is an approximation. Pretrained models (DenseNet-121, ResNet-50, PSPNet, UNet-ResNet50, BiomedCLIP) were used only as cross-checks: the classifiers were inconsistent (e.g., a spurious high pneumothorax score from ResNet-50 contradicted direct visual evidence and was rejected) and BiomedCLIP was non-discriminating, so no finding relies on a model output. A small right subpulmonic effusion cannot be completely excluded as an alternative contributor to the right basal border, though the dome shape and the soft-tissue density below it favor a true elevated diaphragm.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (portable AP appearance) with overlying ECG electrodes and wires. Diffuse bilateral reticular-alveolar (airspace) opacification, patchy and mottled, involving both lung fields, predominant in the mid and lower zones and clearly worse in the right lung than the left, with confluent haziness at the right base. No discrete focal mass or nodule identified. No pneumothorax. No definite pleural effusion: no meniscus sign, and aerated lung is still visible at the left base lateral to the heart; a small right effusion cannot be excluded behind the basal haziness. The cardiac silhouette is partially obscured by adjacent airspace disease and its size cannot be reliably assessed on this single AP view. No endotracheal tube or central venous catheter identified.
impression: Bilateral multifocal airspace disease (infiltrates), right greater than left, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia in a monitored (ICU-type) patient; pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic/ARDS) is the main alternative but the marked asymmetry and mottled consolidation pattern favor infection.
limitations: Single frontal view (likely portable AP); no lateral view and no prior for comparison. Overlying ECG electrodes/wires may obscure small lesions. 8-bit PNG without DICOM metadata (no kVp/mAs, no patient data). Cardiac size not reliably assessable due to AP magnification and obscured borders. A small right pleural effusion cannot be excluded behind the basal haziness. Pretrained model outputs were used only after a bias-control check: scores at or below the structureless-image baseline (notably Mass, Nodule, Pneumothorax, Cardiomegaly, Enlarged Cardiomediastinum) were discounted, and the model's Mass/Nodule signals were not supported by high-magnification visual inspection.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph. Dominant finding: a dense, well-defined, dome-shaped opacity at the left lung base with elevation of the left hemidiaphragm and reduced left lung volume (PSPNet left/right lung area ratio 0.79). The opacity sits between aerated lung above and abdominal gas below. A subtle, small, ill-defined round opacity is present in the right mid-lung zone (possible small nodule or a vessel on end). A small metallic density is seen in the lower abdomen (foreign body / skin marker). The cardiac silhouette appears normal in size (CTR ~0.4); the trachea is midline; no pneumothorax and no clear pleural effusion are identified.
impression: Left basal opacity with elevated left hemidiaphragm, most consistent with left lower lobe atelectasis and/or an elevated (eventrated) left hemidiaphragm. A subtle right mid-zone focus (possible small nodule) is noted. No pneumothorax or clear effusion.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral), so diaphragm elevation versus a retrocardiac/lobar process cannot be fully separated. Breast shadows overlap the lung bases and costophrenic angles. The image is a downsampled 8-bit PNG, limiting fine detail. Pretrained classifier scores for the key labels were weak and partly conflicting (e.g., cardiomegaly 0.64 vs 0.19 between DenseNet and ResNet), so they were used only as corroboration. The community bone-fracture model flagged 'Fractured' (0.89) but no fracture is visible, so that result was rejected. The right mid-zone focus is subtle and its nature (nodule vs vessel) is uncertain.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. Diffuse bilateral mixed alveolar and interstitial pulmonary opacities involving all lung zones, most confluent in the mid and lower zones (labelled Infiltration). A dense, confluent left basilar opacity obscures the left hemidiaphragm and the left heart border and shows a meniscus-like lateral margin, consistent with a left pleural effusion; by contrast the right hemidiaphragm remains visible. The cardiac silhouette appears somewhat prominent on this AP film, but the left heart border is obscured by the adjacent basilar opacity and the approximate cardiothoracic ratio is borderline (~0.42), so cardiomegaly cannot be confirmed. Multiple monitoring and support devices are present (ECG electrodes, a midline line/tube, and external devices over both upper arms). No pneumothorax is identified.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary opacities with a left pleural effusion in a patient carrying multiple support devices. The pattern is most consistent with pulmonary edema (cardiogenic or non-cardiogenic) or a diffuse airspace process such as acute respiratory distress syndrome or multifocal pneumonia; clinical and laboratory correlation is recommended.
limitations: Single portable AP view (no PA or lateral), which magnifies the cardiac silhouette and limits assessment of cardiomegaly; the left basilar opacity obscures the left hemidiaphragm and left heart border, limiting precise delineation of the effusion and the heart. Overlying ECG electrodes, a midline line/tube, and external devices reduce image quality and may mimic or obscure pathology. Pretrained model outputs are supportive only and disagreed between architectures (e.g., edema 0.52 vs 0.19; effusion 0.50 vs 0.13), so they were not used to drive findings. PSPNet anatomical segmentation was unreliable on this opacified image (under-segmented lungs and heart) and was not used for measurement. The etiology of the diffuse opacities (edema vs infection vs ARDS) cannot be determined from a single radiograph and requires clinical correlation.

findings: Portable AP supine chest radiograph of a patient with a tracheostomy tube and external monitoring leads/electrodes. There is a large, dense, homogeneous opacity occupying the right lower hemithorax and extending into the right mid zone, with a relatively flat, slightly concave upper border; it obscures the right hemidiaphragm and the right heart border (silhouette sign), and the thoracic spine is visible through it. A separate, well-demarcated rounded soft-tissue opacity is present in the right mid zone at the level of the right hilum, just above the superior margin of the large basal opacity. The right upper zone shows diffuse hazy increased markings. The left lung is clear with a visible left heart border and hemidiaphragm. The trachea is midline at the level of the tracheostomy. No pneumothorax and no definite displaced rib fracture are seen.
impression: Large right pleural effusion with adjacent atelectasis/consolidation occupying the right lower hemithorax, plus a well-demarcated rounded right hilar/mid-zone opacity (mass). Left lung clear. Portable AP supine geometry limits quantitative assessment.
limitations: Single portable AP supine view: cardiac size and effusion volume cannot be reliably quantified (fluid layers posteriorly), no lateral view, and no prior for comparison. External lines, ECG electrodes and the tracheostomy tube overlie and partially obscure the right lower and left upper fields, and there is patient rotation. The right hemidiaphragm and right costophrenic angle are obscured by the opacity. Pretrained classifiers were trained mostly on PA views: DenseNet-121 failed a gray-blank sanity check (used only as weak corroboration), ResNet-50 passed sanity checks, PSPNet segmentation failed on this image (mask leak, discarded), and BiomedCLIP zero-shot margins are weakly calibrated. The right hilar rounded opacity cannot be fully characterized on a single frontal projection.

findings: Portable AP frontal chest radiograph. Near-complete opacification of the right hemithorax: the right lung is opacified from the upper zone to the base, with multiple round-to-oval low-density areas (approximately 1.5-4 cm, non-air density, partially aerated) clustered in the right mid-lower lung, and residual aeration of the right apex. The right hemidiaphragm and right heart border are obscured (silhouette sign). A thin pigtail (hairpin) drainage catheter is present in the right upper/mid lung, entering from the right infraclavicular/axillary region. The left lung is aerated with a sharp left costophrenic angle and a normal gastric bubble. No pneumothorax and no definite rib fracture are identified. Two external wire-like artifacts overlie the chest soft tissues (crossing the left upper chest and along the right arm/axilla).
impression: Near-complete right hemithorax opacification with multiple cavitating/low-density areas, most consistent with cavitating (necrotizing) pneumonia of the right lung - multiple (partially filled) lung abscesses - with an indwelling pigtail drainage catheter; a large right pleural effusion or complete right lung collapse cannot be excluded on this single view.
limitations: Single portable AP view without lateral view or prior comparison; patient rotation and soft-tissue superimposition at the apices; trachea and mediastinum poorly visualized, so mediastinal shift/volume status could not be assessed; the rounded lucencies are partially aerated (not air density), so cavities may be partially filled and consolidation, effusion and collapse cannot be fully separated on one view; the catheter course below y~550 could not be traced within the opacity; pretrained models were used only as corroborating evidence and out-of-domain tools (pediatric wrist YOLOv8, bone-fracture classifier) were rejected.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (single view, adult). Multiple well-circumscribed rounded nodular opacities in the right mid and lower lung zones, the densest and largest (approximately 10-15 mm) lateral to the mid-lung, with several smaller foci medially; a few small faint foci may represent end-on vessels. Diffuse mottled reticulonodular increased opacity throughout the left lung, most pronounced in the upper and mid zones, without focal consolidation or air bronchogram. Hazy opacity over the right base with partial obscuration of the right hemidiaphragm, mild right hemidiaphragm elevation and slight blunting of the right costophrenic angle (basilar atelectasis; a small effusion cannot be excluded). The right upper zone is relatively hyperlucent; lung markings extend to the chest wall and no pleural line is seen (no pneumothorax). Cardiac silhouette is normal in size (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.3); trachea midline; no mediastinal widening; no acute bony abnormality identified. An external side marker is present at the top right of the image.
impression: Multiple right mid-lower lung zone pulmonary nodules with diffuse mottled left-lung opacities and right basilar atelectasis (possible small effusion). The pattern suggests a multifocal pulmonary process, most likely an infectious multifocal infiltrate with a nodular component; no pneumothorax, no cardiomegaly, no pulmonary edema.
limitations: Single frontal view (no lateral); PA vs AP projection uncertain (possible AP magnification). Image is a display-LUT 8-bit PNG, so absolute densities are limited and classifier inputs may deviate from raw training data. Right upper zone hyperlucency cannot be separated between regional over-penetration and mild emphysema. Right basilar opacity cannot reliably distinguish atelectasis from a small effusion on one view. Nodule sizes are approximate pixel measurements without mm calibration. Small faint foci (two low-confidence boxes) may be end-on vessels. No prior studies for comparison. Pretrained-model outputs were used only as corroboration: their pneumothorax flags were rejected because direct inspection showed lung markings to the periphery with no pleural line; no finding rests on a model alone.

findings: Frontal (PA) chest radiograph. Patchy parenchymal opacities in both lower lung zones, markedly more extensive in the patient-LEFT mid-to-lower zone (hazy reticulonodular opacity with partial obscuration of the left heart border) than in the patient-right medial base. No definite lobar consolidation, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax. Heart size normal by measurement (cardiothoracic ratio 0.38). Medical devices in situ: central venous catheter from the right neck with tip in the superior vena cava/upper right atrium region, a rectangular radiopaque device with an attached lead overlying the right mid lung field (external/implanted hardware), and a coiled tube traversing the right lower zone.
impression: Bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates, left mid-lower zone predominant, most consistent with an infectious/inflammatory process (pneumonia); pulmonary edema is less likely given normal heart size and absence of effusion. Multiple support devices present.
limitations: Single frontal view only (no lateral view to lateralize the opacities). 8-bit PNG without HU scale, so intensities are relative, not quantitative. Superimposed hardware (central line, rectangular device with lead, coiled tube) may obscure or mimic pathology, particularly in the right lower zone. The 18-pathology classifiers (DenseNet121, ResNet50) returned indeterminate scores (raw probabilities below 0.2 for every label), so they served only as cross-checks; BiomedCLIP zero-shot was weakly corroborating; localization therefore rests on direct visual assessment plus segmentation (PSPNet), density thresholding and MedSAM. PSPNet masks leak into the black background at apical/basal rows (corrected) and partially mislabel the hazy right lower zone, so ROI statistics are approximate. No clinical history, laboratory data, or prior imaging available.

findings: AP portable (supine) chest radiograph of a critically ill patient with a tracheostomy tube in situ, a left subclavian dual-lumen central venous catheter with tip projecting over the superior vena cava, and multiple ECG leads. Large confluent hazy-to-dense opacity occupying the right upper and mid lung zones, extending to the apex and obscuring the right upper lung markings, denser medially; no air bronchograms or meniscus visible. Dense homogeneous dependent opacity at the right base obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle. Patchy bilateral airspace opacities in the left mid and lower lung zones. Cardiac silhouette appears prominent, but size is overestimated by AP supine geometry and obscured by adjacent opacities (manual cardiothoracic ratio ~0.38; definite cardiomegaly not confirmed). No pneumothorax, and no displaced rib fracture identified.
impression: Right upper/mid zone consolidation with right basilar pleural effusion and bilateral patchy airspace opacities in a tracheostomized ICU patient; most consistent with pneumonia and pleural effusion, with pulmonary edema/ARDS and atelectasis in the differential; cardiomegaly not confirmed.
limitations: Single AP portable supine view (no PA or lateral comparison); cardiac size assessment limited by AP magnification and adjacent opacities (manual CTR ~0.38; PSPNet-derived CTR is an overestimate because the heart mask over-segments into adjacent opacity). 8-bit re-sampled PNG export rather than original DICOM limits subtle density differences. Overlying ECG leads, tracheostomy and central venous catheter partially obscure the lung fields. Classifier models are out-of-distribution on this portable ICU film: DenseNet 'Mass' (0.67) is contradicted by ResNet50 (0.041) and by image inspection (no discrete mass margins) and was not reported; BiomedCLIP zero-shot similarities were low and only weakly discriminative. Effusion vs consolidation vs atelectasis in the right upper zone cannot be definitively distinguished on a single supine film; MedSAM output is biased by the bounding-box prompt. No contrast-enhanced or CT correlation available.

findings: Single frontal chest radiograph. A left-sided chest tube is in situ: blunt radiopaque tip in the left upper zone (approx x 605, y 156), near-vertical course to approx (616, 400), then curving laterally through the left mid/lower zone, crossing the left lower chest wall with the external portion continuing to the lower right of the image (approx x 923, y 977). A separate short, straight radiopaque object (approx 150 px long) is present in the left lower zone above the left hemidiaphragm (approx x 660-800, y 723-773), isolated from the chest tube except where it crosses; identity uncertain (needle or catheter fragment). An L-shaped radiopaque marker lies over the left shoulder and a thin wire crosses the right upper chest wall from the image's left edge; both are external. Lungs otherwise clear: no definite pneumothorax (no visceral pleural line; pulmonary markings reach the periphery on both sides), no definite pleural effusion, no focal consolidation or mass. Cardiothoracic ratio approx 0.48 (normal). A small (~5 mm) round opacity is seen in the right lower zone at diaphragm level (approx x 325, y 752); possibly a vessel in cross-section, a tiny granuloma, or artifact. No definite rib fracture.
impression: Left chest tube in situ in appropriate position, with a separate short linear radiopaque object of uncertain identity in the left lower zone; no definite acute intrathoracic pathology (no visible pneumothorax, effusion, or consolidation) on this single frontal view.
limitations: Single frontal view without lateral, oblique, or prior films, and without metadata (projection, exposure, patient data); the chest tube overlaps the left lower zone and left costophrenic angle, so a small left effusion or a pneumothorax adjacent to the tube tip cannot be fully excluded. The image is a low-contrast 8-bit export (max 216); classifier outputs on it were shown to be unstable (orientation-, contrast- and tube-dependent) and the models disagree with each other, so no model output supports a finding; BiomedCLIP similarities were non-discriminative; MedSAM failed to segment the thin tube; the wrist-trauma YOLO detector and the community fracture classifier are out of domain and were rejected. The short linear object's identity is uncertain, and the right-base round opacity is indeterminate.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph. Bilateral patchy airspace opacities, most prominent in the lower zones. Two focal rounded opacities: a ~3.5 cm rounded opacity with hazy border in the right mid-lower zone, and a ~3 cm well-defined rounded/lobulated opacity in the left mid zone (the site indicated by the external arrow marker). Dense homogeneous right basal opacity obscuring the right hemidiaphragm and costophrenic angle (consolidation and/or pleural effusion, not separable on this view). Hazy left basal/retrocardiac opacity. Upper zones aerated; no pneumothorax. No definite cardiomegaly on this AP projection (heart-width/thoracic-width ~0.37 from segmentation masks). A radiopaque catheter/tubing courses over the right hemithorax; its tip is not clearly identified.
impression: Multifocal bilateral airspace disease with two focal mass-like rounded opacities (right mid-lower zone and left mid zone). Most likely multifocal pneumonia with rounded areas of consolidation in an acutely ill patient (portable study, indwelling catheter); multifocal metastases or other mass-forming process cannot be excluded without CT.
limitations: Single portable AP view only: cardiac magnification, no lateral view, no prior for comparison, and consolidation cannot be separated from effusion at the right base. Catheter tip position not assessable. The two rounded opacities cannot be definitively characterized (mass vs rounded consolidation vs septic embolus) on a single radiograph; CT is the appropriate next study. Bounding boxes were established by visual inspection of raw/CLAHE crops plus model-assisted segmentation; centimeter size estimates assume ~0.35-0.4 mm/px. Pretrained classifiers partially agree (DenseNet Mass 0.93 vs ResNet Infiltration 0.33) and were used only to guide, not to confirm, findings; zero-shot BiomedCLIP had low discriminative power and was used as weak corroboration only.

findings: Portable supine AP chest radiograph of an intubated patient. Endotracheal tube within the trachea, tip in the upper-mid trachea approximately 4-5 cm above the carina. Multiple ECG electrode snaps and lead wires overlying the chest, a round external device/connector over the right neck, and scattered external metallic fragments over the left upper arm. Diffuse bilateral patchy airspace and interstitial opacities, most prominent in the mid and lower zones bilaterally, hazy and somewhat conflent, more extensive on the left. The cardiac silhouette appears enlarged (cardiothoracic ratio approximately 0.6 by segmented-mask measurement on this film), unreliable on a supine AP projection. Hemidiaphragms appear elevated and the costophrenic angles are obscured (left by overlying arm soft tissue, right by basal opacity); a small effusion cannot be excluded. No pneumothorax is seen and no discrete mass or nodule is identified.
impression: Diffuse bilateral multifocal pulmonary infiltrates (mid and lower zones, left greater than right) in a supine intubated patient, most consistent with multifocal pneumonia and/or pulmonary edema (ARDS); apparent cardiomegaly and small bilateral pleural effusions cannot be excluded on this projection.
limitations: Portable supine AP film: cardiac and mediastinal sizes are overestimated and basal assessment is degraded. Overlying ECG electrodes, lead wires, arm soft tissue and external metallic artifacts degrade the left hemithorax and costophrenic angles; small effusions and basal atelectasis cannot be excluded. Single frontal view, no lateral view. Pretrained multi-label classifiers were poorly calibrated on this film (one flagged all 18 labels) and were used only as corroborating evidence; final bounding boxes were verified visually against crops. Pneumonia versus edema cannot be distinguished from imaging alone and requires clinical context.

findings: Portable supine AP chest radiograph of a patient with multiple indwelling devices: tracheostomy tube in the trachea; a central venous catheter whose tip has coiled into a loop just right of the midline at carinal level (possible kinking/malposition); two pigtail-tipped drainage catheters, one in each hemithorax; two enteric tubes with distal tips in the upper abdomen; three ECG electrodes. Bilateral coarse reticular/interstitial opacities with a patchy airspace component, most prominent in the mid and lower zones (infiltrate/edema pattern). Hazy right (image-left) lower zone opacity with a smooth gradient upper margin reaching the mid-lung, densest at the base, consistent with a pleural effusion layering in the supine position; adjacent atelectasis or consolidation cannot be separated on this single view. Left costophrenic region is relatively lucent; a slight hazy density at the medial left base is not separable from the cardiac and diaphragmatic silhouettes. No pneumothorax: apices are symmetric in density, no visceral pleural line on high-contrast windows, and lung markings reach the periphery. No definite cardiomegaly: manual cardiothoracic ratio about 0.38-0.40.
impression: Diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates (pulmonary edema/ARDS pattern) with a moderate right pleural effusion and basilar atelectasis, in a patient with multiple lines and tubes; no pneumothorax and no definite cardiomegaly.
limitations: Single supine portable AP view: cardiac magnification and elevated diaphragms; effusions layer posteriorly and appear as a diffuse veil, and a small pneumothorax cannot be fully excluded. Heavy overlying hardware (ECG electrodes, tubes, coiled catheter) obscures parts of the lung fields, and an external black bar over the left flank removes part of the image. No prior studies for comparison. Pretrained outputs (DenseNet121, ResNet50, ViewModel, PSPNet, BiomedCLIP, MedSAM) were each validated on this specific image before use; PSPNet masks and several zero-shot BiomedCLIP outputs were found unreliable here and did not support any finding. Weak model signals for pneumothorax (DenseNet 0.52, BiomedCLIP 0.66-1.0) were judged a gestalt response to the ICU-with-drains appearance and were rejected against direct high-contrast inspection. Tube identities and the coiled catheter tip position require clinical correlation; no clinical history was inferred.

findings: Portable AP chest radiograph with multiple external monitoring devices (ECG electrodes and wires) and a right internal jugular/subclavian central venous catheter whose tip projects over the lower SVC. There is a hazy opacity in the left lower zone with a meniscus-shaped upper margin, blunting of the left costophrenic angle, and obscuration of the left hemidiaphragm and the left heart border. The right lung is well aerated with a sharp right costophrenic angle; no right effusion, focal consolidation, nodule, or pneumothorax is seen. No displaced rib fracture is identified. The cardiac silhouette appears prominent, consistent with AP magnification; three independent models do not support cardiomegaly. Incidental small round soft-tissue density in the left upper quadrant, likely a swallowed pill or gastric content.
impression: Left lower zone opacity, most consistent with a small-to-moderate left pleural effusion with associated basilar atelectasis; early consolidation cannot be excluded on this single portable view.
limitations: Single portable AP projection without a lateral view: effusion vs atelectasis vs consolidation cannot be fully differentiated, and the cardiothoracic ratio is not measurable because the left heart border is obscured. Overlying ECG electrodes/wires and an external monitoring device partly obscure the right upper lung and the left lower lateral chest wall. Classifier support for the basilar opacity is only marginal (DenseNet) and the DenseNet 'mass' score proved to be a false positive (clavicle/electrode overlap, intensity-verified); the ResNet 'lung opacity' output was flip-unstable and discounted. PSPNet heart/diaphragm/aorta masks were unreliable on this film and only its lung masks were used. Model outputs served only as corroboration; the finding is based on direct visual inspection of the original and its crops.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph obtained on expiration (lead marker visible). The right hemithorax shows extensive airspace disease in two patterns: (1) a mottled, patchy consolidation of the right mid zone with air-containing pockets (air bronchograms) extending from the lateral chest wall to the paracardiac region, and (2) a dense, homogeneous basal opacity with a concave upper border (measured ~y550 laterally rising to ~y380 medially) that obscures the right hemidiaphragm and the right heart border (silhouette sign) and reaches the lateral chest wall. The left lung is clear at the apex and upper zone with mild basal haziness; a thin, lens-shaped, intermediate-attenuation band in the left mid-lower zone (~x662-750, y547-565) is most consistent with the oblique fissure seen en profile or a normal lucent area - it is denser than adjacent aerated lung and has no pleural line, so it is not a pneumothorax or bulla. The left costophrenic angle is sharp. Trachea is midline without mediastinal shift. The cardiac silhouette is partly obscured; no definite cardiomegaly in this expiratory state. No pleural line or peripheral lucency at either apex (no pneumothorax). No free air under the diaphragm. No rib fracture or other skeletal abnormality identified.
impression: Right mid and lower zone airspace consolidation (pneumonia pattern) with a dense right basal opacity consistent with a right pleural effusion and/or right lower lobe collapse; no pneumothorax or free air.
limitations: Single frontal projection taken on expiration; no paired inspiratory or lateral view, so superimposition cannot be resolved, cardiac size cannot be assessed, and the effusion volume cannot be quantified. The right basal opacity obscures the right hemidiaphragm and right heart border, so the exact mix of effusion vs consolidation vs collapse in the dense component cannot be determined. The expiratory state exaggerates vascular crowding and apparent cardiac size. Pretrained model scores were used only as cross-checks: they vary strongly across training datasets (CheXpert-variant high, RSNA-variant weak), the PSPNet segmentation fails within the opacity, the zero-shot CLIP comparison was non-discriminative, and the wrist-trained YOLO detector was out of domain; none of these were used to establish a finding.

findings: Frontal chest radiograph (AP projection, likely supine) with multiple support devices.
